entries.f7560fffc9957bd67b02b53ceaaac3430594e59c: <div sID="gen25862" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Luke.12" sID="Luke.12"/> <div eID="gen25862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25863" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25864" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have divers excellent discourses of our Saviour's upon various occasions, many of which are to the same purport with what we had in Matthew upon other the like occasions; for we may suppose that our Lord Jesus preached the same doctrines, and pressed the same duties, at several times, in several companies, and that one of the evangelists took them as he delivered them at one time and another at another time; and we need thus to have precept upon precept, line upon line. Here, I. Christ warns his disciples to take heed of hypocrisy, and of cowardice in professing Christianity and preaching the gospel, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.1-Luke.12.12">ver. 1-12</reference>. II. He gives a caution against covetousness, upon occasion of a covetous motion made to him, and illustrates that caution by a parable of a rich man suddenly cut off by death in the midst of his worldly projects and hopes, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.13-Luke.12.21">ver. 13-21</reference>. III. He encourages his disciples to cast all their care upon God, and to live easy in a dependence upon his providence, and exhorts them to make religion their main business, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.22-Luke.12.34">ver. 22-34</reference>. IV. He stirs them up to watchfulness for their Master's coming, from the consideration of the reward of those who are then found faithful, and the punishment of those who are found unfaithful, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.35-Luke.12.48">ver. 35-48</reference>. V. He bids them expect trouble and persecution, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.49-Luke.12.53">ver. 49-53</reference>. VI. He warns the people to observe and improve the day of their opportunities and to make their peace with God in time, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.54-Luke.12.59">ver. 54-59</reference>.
entries.4d0bf30fe54263120607d340308ec231c18d1833: <div eID="gen25864" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25863" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Charge to His Apostles.</title> <div sID="gen25865" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the mean time, when there were gathered together an innumerable multitude of people, insomuch that they trode one upon another, he began to say unto his disciples first of all, Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. 2 For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops. <hi type="super">4</hi> And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. <hi type="super">5</hi> But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell; yea, I say unto you, Fear him. <hi type="super">6</hi> Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God? 7 But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows. <hi type="super">8</hi> Also I say unto you, Whosoever shall confess me before men, him shall the Son of man also confess before the angels of God: <hi type="super">9</hi> But he that denieth me before men shall be denied before the angels of God. <hi type="super">10</hi> And whosoever shall speak a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but unto him that blasphemeth against the Holy Ghost it shall not be forgiven. <hi type="super">11</hi> And when they bring you unto the synagogues, and <hi type="italic">unto</hi> magistrates, and powers, take ye no thought how or what thing ye shall answer, or what ye shall say: <hi type="super">12</hi> For the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour what ye ought to say. <div eID="gen25865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25866" type="x-p"/> We find here, I. A vast auditory that was got together to hear Christ preach. The <hi type="italic">scribes</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees</hi> sought <hi type="italic">to accuse him,</hi> and do him mischief; but the people, who were not under the bias of their prejudices and jealousies, still <hi type="italic">admired</hi> him, attended on him, and did him honour. <hi type="italic">In the mean time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.1">v. 1</reference>), while he was in the Pharisee's house, contending with them that sought to ensnare him, the people got together for an afternoon sermon, a sermon after <hi type="italic">dinner,</hi> after dinner with a Pharisee; and he would not disappoint them. Though in the morning sermon, when they were <hi type="italic">gathered thickly together</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.29">ch. xi. 29</reference>), he had severely reproved them, as an <hi type="italic">evil generation that seek a sign,</hi> yet they renewed their attendance on him; so much better could the people bear <hi type="italic">their</hi> reproofs than the Pharisees <hi type="italic">theirs.</hi> The more the Pharisees strove to drive the people from Christ, the more flocking there was to him. Here was an <hi type="italic">innumerable multitude of people gathered together, so that they trade one upon another,</hi> in labouring to get foremost, and to come within hearing. It is a good sight to see people thus forward to hear the word, and venture upon inconvenience and danger rather than miss an opportunity for their souls. Who are these that thus <hi type="italic">fly as the doves to their windows?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.60.8">Isa. lx. 8</reference>. When the net is cast where there is such a multitude of fish, it may be hoped that some will be enclosed. <div eID="gen25866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25867" type="x-p"/> II. The instructions which he gave his followers, in the hearing of this auditory. <div eID="gen25867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25868" type="x-p"/> 1. He began with a caution against <hi type="italic">hypocrisy.</hi> This he said <hi type="italic">to his disciples first of all;</hi> either to the twelve, or to the seventy. These were his more peculiar charge, his family, his school, and therefore he particularly <hi type="italic">warned them</hi> as his <hi type="italic">beloved sons;</hi> they made more profession of religion than others and hypocrisy in <hi type="italic">that</hi> was the sin they were most in danger of. They were to preach to others; and, if they should <hi type="italic">prevaricate,</hi> corrupt the word, and deal deceitfully, hypocrisy would be worse in them than in others. Besides, there was a Judas among them, who was a hypocrite, and Christ knew it, and would hereby startle him, or leave him inexcusable. Christ's disciples were, for aught we know, the <hi type="italic">best men</hi> then in the world, yet they needed to be cautioned against hypocrisy. Christ said this to the disciples, <hi type="italic">in the hearing</hi> of this great multitude, rather than <hi type="italic">privately</hi> when he had them by themselves, to add the greater weight to the caution, and to let the world know that he would not countenance hypocrisy, no, not in <hi type="italic">his own disciples.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen25868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25869" type="x-p"/> (1.) The description of that sin which he warns them against: <hi type="italic">It is the leaven of the Pharisees.</hi> [1.] It is <hi type="italic">leaven;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">spreading</hi> as leaven, <hi type="italic">insinuates</hi> itself into the whole man, and all that he does; it is <hi type="italic">swelling</hi> and <hi type="italic">souring</hi> as leaven, for it puffs men up with pride, embitters them with malice, and makes their service unacceptable to God. [2.] It is the leaven of the Pharisees: "It is the sin they are most of them found in. Take heed of imitating them; be not you of their spirit; do not dissemble in Christianity as they do in Judaism; make not <hi type="italic">your</hi> religion a <hi type="italic">cloak of maliciousness,</hi> as they do theirs." <div eID="gen25869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25870" type="x-p"/> (2.) A good reason against it: "<hi type="italic">For there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.2-Luke.12.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. It is to no purpose to dissemble, for, sooner or later, truth will come out; and a <hi type="italic">lying tongue is but for a moment.</hi> If you <hi type="italic">speak in darkness</hi> that which is unbecoming you, and is inconsistent with your public professions, <hi type="italic">it shall be heard in the light;</hi> some way or other it shall be discovered, <hi type="italic">a bird of the air shall carry the voice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.20">Eccl. x. 20</reference>), and your folly and falsehood will be <hi type="italic">made manifest.</hi>" The iniquity that is concealed with a show of piety will be discovered, perhaps in this world, as Judas's was, and Simon Magus's, at furthest in the great day, when the <hi type="italic">secrets of all hearts</hi> shall be made <hi type="italic">manifest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.14">Eccl. xii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.16">Rom. ii. 16</reference>. If men's religion prevail not to conquer and cure the wickedness of their hearts, it shall not always serve for a cloak. The day is coming when hypocrites will be stripped of their fig-leaves. <div eID="gen25870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25871" type="x-p"/> 2. To this he added a charge to them to be faithful to the trust reposed in them, and not to betray it, through cowardice or base fear. Some make <reference osisRef="Luke.12.2-Luke.12.3">v. 2, 3</reference>, to be a caution to them not to <hi type="italic">conceal</hi> those things which they had been <hi type="italic">instructed</hi> in, and were <hi type="italic">employed</hi> to publish to the world. "Whether men will <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> or whether they will <hi type="italic">forbear,</hi> tell them the <hi type="italic">truth,</hi> the <hi type="italic">whole</hi> truth, and <hi type="italic">nothing but</hi> the truth; what has been spoken to you, and you have talked of among yourselves, <hi type="italic">privately,</hi> and in corners, that do you preach <hi type="italic">publicly,</hi> whoever is offended; for, if you <hi type="italic">please men,</hi> you are not <hi type="italic">Christ's servants,</hi> nor can you please him," <reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Gal. i. 10</reference>. But this was not the worst of it: it was likely to be a <hi type="italic">suffering</hi> cause, though never a <hi type="italic">sinking</hi> one: let them therefore arm themselves with courage; and divers arguments are furnished here to steel them with a holy resolution in their work. Consider, <div eID="gen25871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25872" type="x-p"/> (1.) "The power of your enemies is a limited power (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">I say unto you, my friends</hi>" (Christ's disciples are his friends, he calls them <hi type="italic">friends,</hi> and gives them this <hi type="italic">friendly</hi> advice), "<hi type="italic">be not afraid,</hi> do not disquiet yourselves with tormenting fears of the power and rage of men." Note, Those whom Christ owns for <hi type="italic">his friends</hi> need not be afraid of any enemies. "<hi type="italic">Be not afraid,</hi> no, not of them that <hi type="italic">kill the body,</hi> let it not be in the power of <hi type="italic">scoffers,</hi> not even of <hi type="italic">murderers,</hi> to drive you off from your work, for you that have learned to triumph over death may say, even of them, Let them do their worst, <hi type="italic">after that there is no more that they can do;</hi> the immortal soul lives, and is happy, and enjoys itself and its God, and sets them all at defiance." Note, Those can do Christ's disciples no real harm, and therefore ought not to be dreaded, who can but <hi type="italic">kill the body;</hi> for they only send that to its rest, and the soul to its joy, the sooner. <div eID="gen25872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25873" type="x-p"/> (2.) God is to be feared more than the most powerful men: "<hi type="italic">I will forewarn you whom you shall fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.5">v. 5</reference>): that you may fear man less, fear God more. Moses conquers his fear of the <hi type="italic">wrath of the king,</hi> by having an eye to him <hi type="italic">that is invisible.</hi> By <hi type="italic">owning Christ</hi> you may incur the wrath of men, which can reach no further than to <hi type="italic">put you to death</hi> (and without God's permission they cannot do that); but by <hi type="italic">denying</hi> Christ, and disowning him, you will incur the wrath of God, which has power to send <hi type="italic">you to hell,</hi> and there is no resisting it. Now of two evils the less is to be chosen, and the greater is to be dreaded, and therefore <hi type="italic">I say unto you, Fear him.</hi>" "It is true," said that blessed martyr, Bishop Hooper, "life is sweet, and death bitter; but eternal life is more sweet, and eternal death more bitter." <div eID="gen25873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25874" type="x-p"/> (3.) The lives of good Christians and good ministers are the particular care of divine Providence, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.6-Luke.12.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. To encourage us in times of difficulty and danger, we must have recourse to our first principles, and build upon them. Now a firm belief of the doctrine of God's universal providence, and the extent of it, will be satisfying to us when at any time we are in peril, and will encourage us to trust God in the way of duty. [1.] Providence takes cognizance of the <hi type="italic">meanest creatures,</hi> even of <hi type="italic">the sparrows.</hi> "Though they are of such small account that <hi type="italic">five</hi> of them are sold for <hi type="italic">two farthings,</hi> yet not one of them is <hi type="italic">forgotten of God,</hi> but is provided for, and notice is taken of its death. Now, <hi type="italic">you are of more value than many sparrows,</hi> and therefore you may be sure you <hi type="italic">are not forgotten,</hi> though imprisoned, though banished, though forgotten by your friends; much more <hi type="italic">precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of saints</hi> than the death of sparrows." [2.] Providence takes cognizance of the <hi type="italic">meanest interest</hi> of the disciples of Christ: "<hi type="italic">Even the very hairs of your head are all numbered</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.7">v. 7</reference>); much more are your sighs and tears numbered, and the drops of your blood, which you shed for Christ's name's sake. An account is kept of all your losses, that they <hi type="italic">may be,</hi> and without doubt they shall be, recompensed unspeakably to your advantage." <div eID="gen25874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25875" type="x-p"/> (4.) "You will be owned or disowned by Christ, in the great day, according as you now own or disown him," <reference osisRef="Luke.12.8-Luke.12.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. [1.] To engage us to <hi type="italic">confess Christ before men,</hi> whatever we may lose or suffer for our constancy to him, and how dear soever it may cost us, we are assured that they who <hi type="italic">confess Christ</hi> now shall be owned by him in the great day <hi type="italic">before the angels of God,</hi> to their everlasting comfort and honour. Jesus Christ will <hi type="italic">confess,</hi> not only that he suffered for them, and that they are to have the benefit of <hi type="italic">his</hi> sufferings, but that they suffered <hi type="italic">for him,</hi> and that his kingdom and interest on earth were advanced by <hi type="italic">their</hi> sufferings; and what greater honour can be done them? [2.] To deter us from <hi type="italic">denying</hi> Christ, and a cowardly <hi type="italic">deserting</hi> of his truths and ways, we are here assured that those who <hi type="italic">deny Christ,</hi> and treacherously depart from him, whatever they may save by it, though it were life itself, and whatever they may gain by it, though it were a kingdom, will be vast losers at last, for they shall be <hi type="italic">denied before the angels of God;</hi> Christ will not know them, will not own them, will not show them any favour, which will turn to their everlasting terror and contempt. By the stress here laid upon their being <hi type="italic">confessed or denied before the angels of God,</hi> it should seem to be a considerable part of the happiness of glorified saints that they will not only stand <hi type="italic">right,</hi> but stand <hi type="italic">high,</hi> in the esteem of the <hi type="italic">holy angels;</hi> they will love them, and honour them, and own them, if they be Christ's servants; they are their fellow-servants, and they will take them for their companions. On the contrary, a considerable part of the misery of damned sinners will be that the holy angels will abandon them, and will be the pleased witnesses, not only of their disgrace, as here, but of their misery, for they shall be <hi type="italic">tormented in the presence of the holy angels</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Rev. xiv. 10</reference>), who will give them no relief. <div eID="gen25875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25876" type="x-p"/> (5.) The errand they were shortly to be sent out upon was of the highest and last importance to the children of men, to whom they were sent, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.10">v. 10</reference>. Let them be bold in preaching the gospel, for a sorer and heavier doom would attend those that rejected them (after the Spirit was poured upon them, which was to be the <hi type="italic">last</hi> method of conviction) than those that now rejected Christ himself, and opposed him: "<hi type="italic">Greater works than those shall he do,</hi> and, consequently, greater will be the punishment of those that blaspheme the gifts and operations of the Holy Ghost in you. <hi type="italic">Whosoever shall speak a word against the Son of man,</hi> shall stumble at the meanness of his appearance, and speak <hi type="italic">slightly</hi> and <hi type="italic">spitefully</hi> of him, it is capable of some excuse: <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.</hi> But unto him that <hi type="italic">blasphemes the Holy Ghost,</hi> that blasphemes the Christian doctrine, and maliciously opposes it, after the pouring out of the Spirit and his attestation of Christ's <hi type="italic">being glorified</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.33">Acts ii. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.32">v. 32</reference>), the privilege of the <hi type="italic">forgiveness of sins</hi> shall be denied; he shall have no benefit by Christ and his gospel. You may shake off the dust of your feet against those that do so, and give them over as incurable; they have forfeited that <hi type="italic">repentance</hi> and that <hi type="italic">remission</hi> which Christ was <hi type="italic">exalted to give,</hi> and which you are <hi type="italic">commissioned to preach.</hi>" The sin, no doubt, was the more daring, and consequently the case the more desperate, during the continuance of the <hi type="italic">extraordinary</hi> gifts and operations of the Spirit in the church, which were intended for a <hi type="italic">sign to them who believed not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.22">1 Cor. xiv. 22</reference>. There were hopes of those who, though not convinced by them at first, yet admired them, but those who <hi type="italic">blasphemed</hi> them were given over. <div eID="gen25876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25877" type="x-p"/> (6.) Whatever trials they should be called out to, they should be sufficiently furnished for them, and honourably brought through them, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.11-Luke.12.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. The faithful martyr for Christ has not only <hi type="italic">sufferings</hi> to <hi type="italic">undergo,</hi> but a <hi type="italic">testimony</hi> to <hi type="italic">bear,</hi> a <hi type="italic">good confession</hi> to <hi type="italic">witness,</hi> and is concerned to do that <hi type="italic">well,</hi> so that the cause of Christ may not suffer, though he suffer for it; and, if this be his care, let him cast it upon God: "When they <hi type="italic">bring you into the synagogues,</hi> before church-rulers, before the Jewish courts, or before <hi type="italic">magistrates and powers,</hi> Gentile rulers, rulers in the state, to be examined about your doctrine, what it is, and what the proof of it, <hi type="italic">take no thought what ye shall answer,</hi>" [1.] "That you may <hi type="italic">save yourselves.</hi> Do not study by what art or rhetoric to mollify your judges, or by what tricks in law to bring yourselves off; if it be the will of God that you should come off, and your time is not yet come, he will bring it about effectually." [2.] "That you may <hi type="italic">serve your Master;</hi> aim at this, but do not perplex yourselves about it, for <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost,</hi> as a Spirit of wisdom, <hi type="italic">shall teach you what you ought to say,</hi> and how to say it, so that it may be for the honour of God and his cause."
entries.a32bad680f82742202d40a47dd700bf3ce3ad689: <div eID="gen25877" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Worldly-mindedness Exposed.</title> <div sID="gen25878" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And one of the company said unto him, Master, speak to my brother, that he divide the inheritance with me. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he said unto him, Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you? <hi type="super">15</hi> And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully: <hi type="super">17</hi> And he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits? 18 And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods. <hi type="super">19</hi> And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, <hi type="italic">and</hi> be merry. <hi type="super">20</hi> But God said unto him, <hi type="italic">Thou</hi> fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? <hi type="super">21</hi> So <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God. <div eID="gen25878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25879" type="x-p"/> We have in these verses, <div eID="gen25879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25880" type="x-p"/> I. The application that was made to Christ, very unseasonably, by one of his hearers, desiring him to interpose <hi type="italic">between him and his brother</hi> in a matter that concerned the estate of the family (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Master, speak to my brother;</hi> speak as a prophet, speak as a king, speak with authority; he is one that will have regard to what thou sayest; speak to him, <hi type="italic">that he divide the inheritance with me.</hi>" Now, 1. Some think that his brother <hi type="italic">did him wrong,</hi> and that he appealed to Christ to <hi type="italic">right him,</hi> because he knew the law was costly. His brother was such a one as the Jews called <hi type="italic">Ben-hamesen</hi>—<hi type="italic">a son of violence,</hi> that took not only his own part of the estate, but his brother's too, and forcibly detained it from him. Such brethren there are in the world, who have no sense at all either of <hi type="italic">natural equity</hi> or <hi type="italic">natural affection,</hi> who make a prey of those whom they ought to patronize and protect. They who are so wronged have God to go to, who will <hi type="italic">execute</hi> judgment and justice for <hi type="italic">those that are oppressed.</hi> 2. Others think that he had a mind to <hi type="italic">do his brother wrong,</hi> and would have Christ to <hi type="italic">assist him;</hi> that, whereas the law gave the elder brother a double portion of the estate, and the father himself could not dispose of what he had but by that rule (<reference osisRef="Deut.21.16-Deut.21.17">Deut. xxi. 16, 17</reference>), he would have Christ to <hi type="italic">alter that law,</hi> and oblige his brother, who perhaps was a follower of Christ at large, to <hi type="italic">divide the inheritance</hi> equally <hi type="italic">with him,</hi> in gavel-kind, share and share alike, and to allot him as much as his elder brother. I suspect that this was the case, because Christ takes occasion from it to warn against <hi type="italic">covetousness,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pleonexia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a desire of having more,</hi> more than God in his providence has allotted us. It was not a lawful desire of getting his own, but a <hi type="italic">sinful</hi> desire of getting more than his own. <div eID="gen25880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25881" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's refusal to interpose in this matter (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Man, who made me a judge or divider over you?</hi> In matters of this nature, Christ will not assume either a <hi type="italic">legislative</hi> power to alter the settled rule of inheritances, or a <hi type="italic">judicial</hi> power to determine controversies concerning them. He could have done the judge's part, and the lawyer's, as well as he did the physician's, and have ended suits at law as happily as he did diseases; but he would not, for it was not in his commission: <hi type="italic">Who made me a judge?</hi> Probably he refers to the indignity done to Moses by his brethren in Egypt, with which Stephen upbraided the Jews, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.27">Acts vii. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.35">35</reference>. "If I should offer to do this, you would taunt me as you did Moses, <hi type="italic">Who made thee a judge or a divider?</hi>" He corrects the man's mistake, will not admit his appeal (it was <hi type="italic">coram non judice—not before the proper judge</hi>), and so <hi type="italic">dismisses</hi> his bill. If he had come to him to desire him to assist his pursuit of the heavenly inheritance, Christ would have given him his best help; but as to this matter he has nothing to do: <hi type="italic">Who made me a judge?</hi> Note, Jesus Christ was no usurper; he took no honour, no power, to himself, but what was given him, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.5">Heb. v. 5</reference>. Whatever he did, he could tell by what authority he did it, and who gave him that authority. Now this shows us what is the nature and constitution of Christ's kingdom. It is a spiritual kingdom, and not of this world. 1. It does not interfere with civil powers, nor take the authority of princes out of their hands. Christianity leaves the matter as it found it, as to civil power. 2. It does not intermeddle with civil rights; it obliges all to do justly, according to the settled rules of equity, but dominion is not founded in grace. 3. It does not <hi type="italic">encourage</hi> our <hi type="italic">expectations</hi> of worldly advantages by our religion. If this man will be a disciple of Christ, and expects that in consideration of this Christ should give him his brother's estate, he is mistaken; the rewards of Christ's disciples are of another nature. 4. It does not <hi type="italic">encourage</hi> our <hi type="italic">contests</hi> with our brethren, and our being rigorous and high in our demands, but rather, for peace' sake, to recede from our right. 5. It does not allow ministers to <hi type="italic">entangle</hi> themselves in the affairs of this <hi type="italic">life</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.4">2 Tim. ii. 4</reference>), to <hi type="italic">leave the word of God to serve tables.</hi> There are those whose business it is, let it be left to them, <hi type="italic">Tractent fabrilia fabri</hi>—<hi type="italic">Each workman to his proper craft.</hi> <div eID="gen25881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25882" type="x-p"/> III. The necessary caution which Christ took occasion from this to give to his hearers. Though he came not to be a <hi type="italic">divider</hi> of men's estates, he came to be a director of their consciences about them, and would have all take heed of harbouring that corrupt principle which they saw to be in others the <hi type="italic">root</hi> of <hi type="italic">so much evil.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen25882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25883" type="x-p"/> 1. The caution itself (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Take heed and beware of covetousness;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">horate</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">Observe yourselves,</hi> keep a <hi type="italic">jealous eye</hi> upon your own hearts, lest covetous principles steal into them; and <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">phylassesthe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">preserve yourselves,</hi> keep a <hi type="italic">strict band</hi> upon your own hearts, lest covetous principles rule and give law in them." Covetousness is a sin which we have need constantly to <hi type="italic">watch against,</hi> and therefore frequently to be <hi type="italic">warned against.</hi> <div eID="gen25883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25884" type="x-p"/> 2. The reason of it, or an argument to enforce this caution: <hi type="italic">For a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth;</hi> that is, "our happiness and comfort do not depend upon our having a great deal of the wealth of this world." (1.) The life of the <hi type="italic">soul,</hi> undoubtedly, does not depend upon it, and the soul is the man. The things of the world will not suit the nature of a soul, nor supply its needs, nor satisfy its desires, nor last so long as it will last. Nay, (2.) Even the life of the body and the happiness of that do not consist in an <hi type="italic">abundance</hi> of these things; for many live very contentedly and easily, and get through the world very comfortably, who have but a little of the wealth of it (a dinner of herbs with holy love is better than a <hi type="italic">feast of fat things</hi>); and, on the other hand, many live very miserably who have a great deal of the things of this world; they possess abundance, and yet have no comfort of it; they <hi type="italic">bereave their souls of good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.8">Eccl. iv. 8</reference>. Many who have abundance are discontented and fretful, as Ahab and Haman; and then what good does their abundance do them? <div eID="gen25884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25885" type="x-p"/> 3. The illustration of this by a parable, the sum of which is to show the folly of carnal worldlings while they live, and their misery when they die, which is intended not only for a check to that man who came to Christ with an address about his estate, while he was in no care about his soul and another world, but for the enforcing of that necessary caution to us all, to <hi type="italic">take heed of covetousness.</hi> The parable gives us the life and death of a <hi type="italic">rich man,</hi> and leaves us to judge whether he was a <hi type="italic">happy</hi> man. <div eID="gen25885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25886" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is an account of his worldly wealth and abundance (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">chora</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">regio</hi>—<hi type="italic">the country.</hi> He had a whole country to himself, a lordship of his own; he was a little prince. Observe, His wealth lay much in the fruits of the earth, for <hi type="italic">the king himself is served by the field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.9">Eccl. v. 9</reference>. He had a great deal of ground, and his ground was <hi type="italic">fruitful;</hi> much would have <hi type="italic">more,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">had more.</hi> Note, The fruitfulness of the earth is a great blessing, but it is a blessing which God often gives plentifully to wicked men, to whom it is a snare, that we may not think to judge of his love or hatred by what is before us. <div eID="gen25886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25887" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here are the workings of his heart, in the midst of this abundance. We are here told what <hi type="italic">he thought within himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.17">v. 17</reference>. Note, The God of heaven knows and observes whatever we think within ourselves, and we are accountable to him for it. He is both a discerner and judge of the thoughts and intents of the heart. We mistake if we imagine that thoughts are <hi type="italic">hid</hi> and thoughts are <hi type="italic">free.</hi> Let us here observe, <div eID="gen25887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25888" type="x-p"/> [1.] What his <hi type="italic">cares</hi> and <hi type="italic">concerns</hi> were. When he saw an extraordinary crop upon his ground, instead of <hi type="italic">thanking God</hi> for it, or rejoicing in the opportunity it would give him of doing the more good, he afflicts himself with this thought, <hi type="italic">What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits?</hi> He speaks as one <hi type="italic">at a loss,</hi> and full of perplexity. <hi type="italic">What shall I do now?</hi> The poorest beggar in the country, that did not know where to get a meal's meat, could not have said a more anxious word. Disquieting care is the common fruit of an abundance of this world, and the common fault of those that have abundance. The more men have, the more perplexity they have with it, and the more solicitous they are to keep what they have and to add to it, how to spare and how to spend; so that even the <hi type="italic">abundance</hi> of the rich will not suffer them to <hi type="italic">sleep,</hi> for thinking what they shall do with what they have and how they shall dispose of it. The rich man seems to speak it with a sigh, <hi type="italic">What shall I do?</hi> And if you ask, Why, what is the matter? Truly he had <hi type="italic">abundance</hi> of wealth, and wants a place to <hi type="italic">put it in,</hi> that is all. <div eID="gen25888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25889" type="x-p"/> [2.] What his <hi type="italic">projects</hi> and <hi type="italic">purposes</hi> were, which were the result of his cares, and were indeed absurd and foolish like them (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">This will I do,</hi> and it is the wisest course I can take, <hi type="italic">I will pull down my barns,</hi> for they are too little, and I will <hi type="italic">build greater, and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods,</hi> and then I shall be at ease." Now here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It was folly for him to call the fruits of the ground <hi type="italic">his</hi> fruits and <hi type="italic">his</hi> goods. He seems to lay a pleasing emphasis upon that, <hi type="italic">my</hi> fruits and <hi type="italic">my</hi> goods; whereas what we have is but <hi type="italic">lent</hi> us for our use, the property is still in God; we are but stewards of our <hi type="italic">Lord's goods,</hi> tenants at will of our Lord's land. It is <hi type="italic">my corn</hi> (saith God) and <hi type="italic">my wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8-Hos.2.9">Hos. ii. 8, 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It was folly for him to <hi type="italic">hoard up</hi> what he had, and then to think it <hi type="italic">well bestowed.</hi> There will I bestow it <hi type="italic">all;</hi> as if none must be bestowed upon the poor, none upon his family, none upon the Levite and <hi type="italic">the stranger,</hi> the <hi type="italic">fatherless and the widow,</hi> but all in the great barn. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It was folly for him to let his <hi type="italic">mind</hi> rise with his <hi type="italic">condition;</hi> when his ground brought forth more plentifully than usual, then to talk of bigger barns, as if the next year must needs be as fruitful as this, and much more abundant, whereas the barn might be as much too big the next year as it was too little this. Years of famine commonly follow years of plenty, as they did in Egypt; and therefore it were better to <hi type="italic">stack</hi> some of his corn for this once. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It was folly for him to think to ease his care by building new barns, for the building of them would but increase his care; those know this who know any thing of the spirit of building. The way that God prescribes for the cure of inordinate care is certainly successful, but the way of the world does but increase it. Besides, when he had done this, there were other cares that would still attend him; the greater the barns, still the greater the cares, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">Eccl. v. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> It was folly for him to contrive and resolve all this <hi type="italic">absolutely</hi> and <hi type="italic">without reserve.</hi> This <hi type="italic">I will</hi> do: <hi type="italic">I will</hi> pull down my barns and will build greater, yea, that <hi type="italic">I will;</hi> without so much as that necessary proviso, <hi type="italic">If the Lord will, I shall live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.4.13-Jas.4.15">Jam. iv. 13-15</reference>. Peremptory projects are foolish projects; for our times are in God's hand, and not in our own, and we do not so much as <hi type="italic">know what shall be on the morrow.</hi> <div eID="gen25889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25890" type="x-p"/> [3.] What his <hi type="italic">pleasing hopes</hi> and <hi type="italic">expectations</hi> were, when he should have made good these projects. "Then <hi type="italic">I will say to my soul,</hi> upon the credit of this security, whether God say it or no, <hi type="italic">Soul,</hi> mark what I say, <hi type="italic">thou hast much goods laid up for many years</hi> in these barns; now <hi type="italic">take thine ease,</hi> enjoy thyself, <hi type="italic">eat, drink, and be merry,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Luke.12.19">v. 19</reference>. Here also appears his folly, as much in the enjoyment of his wealth as in the pursuit of it. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It was folly for him to put off his comfort in his abundance till he had compassed his projects concerning it. When he has built bigger barns, and filled them (which will be a work of time), then he will <hi type="italic">take his ease;</hi> and might he not as well have <hi type="italic">done that now?</hi> Grotius here quotes the story of Pyrrhus, who was projecting to make himself master of Sicily, Africa, and other places, in the prosecution of his victories. Well, says his friend Cyneas, and what must we do then? <hi type="italic">Postea vivemus,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">Then we will live; At hoc jam licet,</hi> says Cyneas, <hi type="italic">We may live now if we please. Secondly,</hi> It was folly for him to be confident that his goods were <hi type="italic">laid up for many years,</hi> as if his bigger barns would be <hi type="italic">safer</hi> than those he had; whereas in an hour's time they might be burnt to the ground and all that was laid up in them, perhaps by lightning, against which there is no defence. A few years may make a great change; <hi type="italic">moth and rust may corrupt, or thieves break through and steal. Thirdly,</hi> It was folly for him to count upon certain <hi type="italic">ease,</hi> when he had laid up abundance of the wealth of this world, whereas there are many things that may make people uneasy in the midst of their greatest abundance. One dead fly may spoil a whole pot of precious ointment; and one thorn a whole bed of down. Pain and sickness of body, disagreeableness of relations, and especially a guilty conscience, may rob a man of his ease, who has ever so much of the wealth of this world. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It was folly for him to think of making no other use of his plenty than to <hi type="italic">eat</hi> and <hi type="italic">drink,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">be merry;</hi> to indulge the flesh, and gratify the sensual appetite, without any thought of doing good to others, and being put thereby into a better capacity of serving God and his generation: as if we <hi type="italic">lived</hi> to <hi type="italic">eat,</hi> and did not <hi type="italic">eat</hi> to <hi type="italic">live,</hi> and the happiness of man consisted in nothing else but in having all the gratifications of sense wound up to the height of pleasurableness. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> It was the greatest folly of all to say all this to his <hi type="italic">soul.</hi> if he had said, <hi type="italic">Body, take thine ease,</hi> for <hi type="italic">thou hast goods laid up for many years,</hi> there had been sense in it; but the soul, considered as an immortal spirit, separable from the body, was no way interested in a barn full of corn or a bag full of gold. If he had had the <hi type="italic">soul of a swine,</hi> he might have <hi type="italic">blessed it</hi> with the satisfaction of <hi type="italic">eating</hi> and <hi type="italic">drinking;</hi> but what is this to the <hi type="italic">soul of a man,</hi> that has exigencies and desires which these things will be no ways suited to? It is the great absurdity which the children of this world are guilty of that they portion their souls in the wealth of the world and the pleasures of sense. <div eID="gen25890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25891" type="x-p"/> (3.) Here is God's sentence upon all this; and we are sure that his judgment is according to truth. He said to himself, said to his soul, <hi type="italic">Take thine ease.</hi> If God had said so too, the man had been happy, as his Spirit witnesses with the spirit of believers to make them easy. <hi type="italic">But God said</hi> quite otherwise; and by his judgment of us we must stand or fall, not by ours of ourselves, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3-1Cor.4.4">1 Cor. iv. 3, 4</reference>. His neighbours blessed him (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Ps. x. 3</reference>), praised him as <hi type="italic">doing well for himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.18">Ps. xlix. 18</reference>); but God said he did ill for himself: <hi type="italic">Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">v. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">God said to him,</hi> that is, decreed this concerning him, and let him know it, either by his conscience or by some awakening providence, or rather by both together. This was said when he was <hi type="italic">in the fulness of his sufficiency</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.22">Job xx. 22</reference>), when his eyes were held waking upon his bed with his cares and contrivances about enlarging his barns, not by adding a bay or two more of building to them, which might serve to answer the end, but by pulling them down and building greater, which was requisite to please his fancy. When he was forecasting this, and had brought it to an issue, and then lulled himself asleep again with a pleasing dream of many years' enjoyment of his present improvements, <hi type="italic">then</hi> God said this to him. Thus Belshazzar was struck with terror by the hand-writing on the wall, in the midst of his jollity. Now observe what God said, <div eID="gen25891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25892" type="x-p"/> [1.] The character he gave him: <hi type="italic">Thou fool,</hi> thou <hi type="italic">Nabal,</hi> alluding to the story of Nabal, that <hi type="italic">fool</hi> (Nabal is his name, and folly is with him) whose heart was struck dead <hi type="italic">as a stone</hi> while he was regaling himself in the abundance of his provision for his sheep-shearers. Note, Carnal worldlings are fools, and the day is coming when God will call them by their own name, <hi type="italic">Thou fool,</hi> and they will call themselves so. <div eID="gen25892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25893" type="x-p"/> [2.] The sentence he passed upon him, a sentence of death: <hi type="italic">This night thy soul shall be required of thee; they shall require thy soul</hi> (so the words are), and then <hi type="italic">whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?</hi> He thought he had goods that should be his for many years, but he must part from them <hi type="italic">this night;</hi> he thought he should enjoy them himself, but he must leave them to he knows not who. Note, The death of carnal worldlings is miserable in itself and terrible to them. <div eID="gen25893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25894" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is a <hi type="italic">force,</hi> an <hi type="italic">arrest;</hi> it is the <hi type="italic">requiring of the soul,</hi> that soul that thou art making such a fool of; what hast thou to do with a soul, who canst use it no better? Thy soul shall be <hi type="italic">required;</hi> this intimates that he is loth to part with it. A good man, who has taken his heart off from this world, cheerfully resigns his soul at death, and gives it up; but a worldly man has it <hi type="italic">torn</hi> from him with violence; it is a terror to him to think of leaving this world. <hi type="italic">They shall require thy soul.</hi> God shall require it; he shall require an account of it. "Man, woman, what hast thou done with thy soul. Give an account of that stewardship." <hi type="italic">They shall;</hi> that is, evil angels as the messengers of God's justice. As good angels receive gracious souls to carry them to their joy, so evil angels receive wicked souls to carry them to the place of torment; they shall <hi type="italic">require it</hi> as a guilty soul to be punished. The devil requires thy soul as his own, for it did, in effect, give itself to him. <div eID="gen25894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25895" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a <hi type="italic">surprize,</hi> an <hi type="italic">unexpected</hi> force. It is in <hi type="italic">the night,</hi> and terrors in the night are most terrible. The time of death is day-time to a good man; it is his morning. But it is night to a worldling, a dark night; he <hi type="italic">lies down in sorrow.</hi> It is <hi type="italic">this night,</hi> this <hi type="italic">present</hi> night, without delay; there is no giving bail, or begging a day. This <hi type="italic">pleasant</hi> night, when thou art promising thyself many years to come, now thou must die, and go to judgment. Thou art entertaining thyself with the fancy of many a merry day, and merry night, and merry feast; but, in the midst of all, here is an end of all, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.4">Isa. xxi. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen25895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25896" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is the leaving of all <hi type="italic">those things</hi> behind <hi type="italic">which they have provided,</hi> which they have laboured for, and prepared for hereafter, with abundance of toil and care. All that which they have placed their happiness in, and built their hope upon, and raised their expectations from, they must leave behind. <hi type="italic">Their pomp shall not descend after them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">Ps. xlix. 17</reference>), but they shall go as naked out of the world as they came into it, and they shall have no benefit at all by what they have hoarded up either in death, in judgment, or in their everlasting state. <div eID="gen25896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25897" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It is leaving them to they <hi type="italic">know not who:</hi> "Then <hi type="italic">whose shall those things be?</hi> Not <hi type="italic">thine</hi> to be sure, and thou knowest not what <hi type="italic">they</hi> will prove for whom thou didst design them, thy children and relations, whether they will be <hi type="italic">wise</hi> or <hi type="italic">fools</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.18-Eccl.2.19">Eccl. ii. 18, 19</reference>), whether such as will bless thy memory or curse it, be a credit to thy family or a blemish, do good or hurt with what thou leavest them, keep it or spend it; nay, thou knowest not but those for whom thou dost design it may be prevented from the enjoyment of it, and it may be turned to somebody else thou little thinkest of; nay, though thou knowest to whom thou leavest it, thou knowest not to whom they will leave it, or into whose hand it will come at last." If many a man could have foreseen to whom his house would have come after his death, he would rather have burned it than beautified it. <div eID="gen25897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25898" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> It is a demonstration of his folly. Carnal worldlings are <hi type="italic">fools</hi> while they live: <hi type="italic">this their way is their folly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.13">Ps. xlix. 13</reference>); but their folly is made most evident when they die: <hi type="italic">at his end he shall be a fool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.11">Jer. xvii. 11</reference>); for then it will appear that he took pains to lay up treasure in a world he was hastening from, but took no care to lay it up in the world he was hastening to. <div eID="gen25898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25899" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Here is the application of this parable (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">So is he,</hi> such a fool, a fool in God's judgment, a fool upon record, that <hi type="italic">layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich towards God.</hi> This is the way and this is the end of such a man. Observe here, <div eID="gen25899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25900" type="x-p"/> 1. The description of a worldly man: He <hi type="italic">lays up treasure for himself,</hi> for the body, for the world, for <hi type="italic">himself</hi> in opposition to God, for that <hi type="italic">self</hi> that is to be <hi type="italic">denied.</hi> (1.) It is his error that he counts his <hi type="italic">flesh himself,</hi> as if the <hi type="italic">body</hi> were the <hi type="italic">man.</hi> If <hi type="italic">self</hi> be rightly stated and understood, it is only the true Christian that lays up treasure for himself, and is <hi type="italic">wise for himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.9.12">Prov. ix. 12</reference>. (2.) It is his error that he makes it his business to <hi type="italic">lay up for the flesh,</hi> which he calls laying up <hi type="italic">for himself.</hi> All his labour is <hi type="italic">for his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">Eccl. vi. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">making provision for the flesh.</hi> (3.) It is his error that he counts those things his <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> which are thus <hi type="italic">laid up</hi> for the world, and the body, and the life that now is; they are the wealth he trusts to, and spends upon, and lets out his affections toward. (4.) The greatest error of all is that he is in no care to be <hi type="italic">rich towards God,</hi> rich in the <hi type="italic">account of God,</hi> whose accounting us rich makes us so (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.9">Rev. ii. 9</reference>), rich in the <hi type="italic">things of God,</hi> rich <hi type="italic">in faith</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jam. ii. 5</reference>), rich in <hi type="italic">good works,</hi> in the <hi type="italic">fruits of righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.18">1 Tim. vi. 18</reference>), rich in graces, and comforts, and spiritual gifts. Many who have abundance of this world are wholly destitute of that which will enrich their souls, which will make them rich towards God, rich for eternity. <div eID="gen25900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25901" type="x-p"/> 2. The folly and misery of a worldly man: <hi type="italic">So is he.</hi> Our Lord Jesus Christ, who knows what the end of things will be, has here told us what his end will be. Note, It is the unspeakable folly of the most of men to mind and pursue the wealth of this world more than the wealth of the other world, that which is merely for the body and for time, more than that which is for the soul and eternity.
entries.a069c5e302a514936ca5ed11e802610f7403f0df: <div eID="gen25901" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Inordinate Care Reproved.</title> <div sID="gen25902" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And he said unto his disciples, Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat; neither for the body, what ye shall put on. <hi type="super">23</hi> The life is more than meat, and the body <hi type="italic">is more</hi> than raiment. <hi type="super">24</hi> Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them: how much more are ye better than the fowls? <hi type="super">25</hi> And which of you with taking thought can add to his stature one cubit? <hi type="super">26</hi> If ye then be not able to do that thing which is least, why take ye thought for the rest? <hi type="super">27</hi> Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not; and yet I say unto you, that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <hi type="super">28</hi> If then God so clothe the grass, which is to day in the field, and to morrow is cast into the oven; how much more <hi type="italic">will he clothe</hi> you, O ye of little faith? <hi type="super">29</hi> And seek not ye what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink, neither be ye of doubtful mind. <hi type="super">30</hi> For all these things do the nations of the world seek after: and your Father knoweth that ye have need of these things. <hi type="super">31</hi> But rather seek ye the kingdom of God; and all these things shall be added unto you. <hi type="super">32</hi> Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. <hi type="super">33</hi> Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth. <hi type="super">34</hi> For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. <hi type="super">35</hi> Let your loins be girded about, and <hi type="italic">your</hi> lights burning; <hi type="super">36</hi> And ye yourselves like unto men that wait for their lord, when he will return from the wedding; that when he cometh and knocketh, they may open unto him immediately. <hi type="super">37</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them. <hi type="super">38</hi> And if he shall come in the second watch, or come in the third watch, and find <hi type="italic">them</hi> so, blessed are those servants. <hi type="super">39</hi> And this know, that if the goodman of the house had known what hour the thief would come, he would have watched, and not have suffered his house to be broken through. <hi type="super">40</hi> Be ye therefore ready also: for the Son of man cometh at an hour when ye think not. <div eID="gen25902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25903" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus is here inculcating some needful useful lessons upon his disciples, which he had before taught them, and had occasion afterwards to press upon them; for they need to have <hi type="italic">precept upon precept, and line upon line: "Therefore,</hi> because there are so many that are ruined by covetousness, and an inordinate affection to the wealth of this world, <hi type="italic">I say unto you,</hi> my disciples, take heed of it." <hi type="italic">Thou, O man of God, flee these things,</hi> as well as thou, O man of the world, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.11">1 Tim. vi. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen25903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25904" type="x-p"/> I. He charges them not to afflict themselves with disquieting perplexing cares about the necessary supports of life: <hi type="italic">Take no thought for your life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.22">v. 22</reference>. In the foregoing parable he had given us warning against that branch of covetousness of which rich people are most in danger; and that is, a <hi type="italic">sensual complacency</hi> in the abundance of this world's goods. Now his disciples might think they were in no danger of this, for they had no plenty or variety to glory in; and therefore he here warns them against another branch of covetousness, which they are most in temptation to that have but a little of this world, which was the case of the disciples at best and much more now that they had left all to follow Christ, and that was, an <hi type="italic">anxious solicitude</hi> about the necessary supports of life: "<hi type="italic">Take no thought for your life,</hi> either for the preservation of it, if it be in danger, or for the provision that is to be made for it, either of food or clothing, <hi type="italic">what ye shall eat</hi> or <hi type="italic">what ye shall put on.</hi>" This is the caution he had largely insisted upon, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Matt. vi. 25</reference>, &c.; and the arguments here used are much the same, designed for our encouragement to cast all our care upon God, which is the <hi type="italic">right way</hi> to <hi type="italic">ease</hi> ourselves of it. Consider then, <div eID="gen25904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25905" type="x-p"/> 1. God, who has done the greater for us, may be depended upon to do the less. He has, without any care or forecast of our own, given us <hi type="italic">life</hi> and a <hi type="italic">body,</hi> and therefore we may cheerfully leave it to him to provide <hi type="italic">meat</hi> for the support of that life, and <hi type="italic">raiment</hi> for the defence of that body. <div eID="gen25905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25906" type="x-p"/> 2. God, who provides for the inferior creatures, may be depended upon to provide for good Christians. "Trust God for <hi type="italic">meat,</hi> for he <hi type="italic">feeds the ravens</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.24">v. 24</reference>); they <hi type="italic">neither sow nor reap,</hi> they take neither care nor pains beforehand to provide for themselves, and yet they are <hi type="italic">fed,</hi> and never perish for want. Now consider <hi type="italic">how much better ye are than the fowls,</hi> than the ravens. Trust God for clothing, for he clothes the lilies (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.27-Luke.12.28">v. 27, 28</reference>); they make no preparation for their own clothing, they <hi type="italic">toil not,</hi> they <hi type="italic">spin not,</hi> the root in the ground is a naked thing, and without ornament, and yet, as the flower grows up, it appears wonderfully <hi type="italic">beautified.</hi> Now, if God has so clothed the flowers, which are fading perishing things, <hi type="italic">shall he not much more clothe</hi> you with such clothing as is fit for you, and with clothing suited to your nature, as theirs is?" When God fed Israel with <hi type="italic">manna</hi> in the wilderness, he also took care for their clothing; for though he did not furnish them with new clothes, yet (which came all to one) he provided that those they had should not <hi type="italic">wax old upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.8.4">Deut. viii. 4</reference>. Thus will he clothe his spiritual Israel; but then let them not be <hi type="italic">of little faith.</hi> Note, Our inordinate cares are owing to the weakness of our faith; for a powerful practical belief of the all-sufficiency of God, his covenant-relation to us as a Father, and especially his precious promises, relating both to this life and that to come, would be mighty, through God, to the pulling down of the strong holds of these disquieting perplexing imaginations. <div eID="gen25906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25907" type="x-p"/> 3. Our cares are fruitless, vain, and insignificant, and therefore it is folly to indulge them. They will not gain us our wishes, and therefore ought not to hinder our repose (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Which of you by taking thought can add to his stature one cubit,</hi> or one inch, can add to <hi type="italic">his age</hi> one year or one hour? Now if ye be <hi type="italic">not able to do that which is least,</hi> if it be not in your power to alter your statures, why should you perplex yourselves about other things, which are as much out of your power, and about which it is necessary that we refer ourselves to the providence of God?" Note, As in our <hi type="italic">stature,</hi> so in our <hi type="italic">state,</hi> it is our wisdom to take <hi type="italic">it as it is,</hi> and make the best of it; for fretting and vexing, carping and caring, will not mend it. <div eID="gen25907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25908" type="x-p"/> 4. An inordinate anxious pursuit of the things of this world, even necessary things, very ill becomes the disciples of Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.29-Luke.12.30">v. 29, 30</reference>): "Whatever others do, <hi type="italic">seek not ye what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink;</hi> do not you afflict yourselves with perplexing cares, nor weary yourselves with constant toils; do not hurry hither and thither with enquiries <hi type="italic">what you shall eat or drink,</hi> as David's enemies, that <hi type="italic">wandered up and down for meat</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.15">Ps. lix. 15</reference>), or as the eagle that <hi type="italic">seeks the prey afar off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.29">Job xxxix. 29</reference>. Let not the disciples of Christ thus <hi type="italic">seek</hi> their food, but ask it of God day by day; let them not be <hi type="italic">of doubtful mind;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">me meteorizesthe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Be not as meteors in the air,</hi> that are blown hither and thither with every wind; do not, like them, <hi type="italic">rise</hi> and <hi type="italic">fall,</hi> but maintain a consistency with yourselves; be even and steady, and have your hearts fixed; <hi type="italic">live not in careful suspense;</hi> let not your minds be continually perplexed between hope and fear, ever upon the rack." Let not the children of God make themselves uneasy; for, <div eID="gen25908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25909" type="x-p"/> (1.) This is to make themselves like the children of this world: "<hi type="italic">All these things do the nations of the world seek after,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.30">v. 30</reference>. They that take care for the body only, and not for the soul, for this world only, and not for the other, look no further than what they shall <hi type="italic">eat</hi> and <hi type="italic">drink;</hi> and, having no all-sufficient God to seek to and confide in, they burden themselves with anxious cares about those things. But it ill becomes you to do so. You, who are called out of the world, ought not to be thus conformed to the world, and to <hi type="italic">walk in the way of this people,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.8.11-Isa.8.12">Isa. viii. 11, 12</reference>. When inordinate cares prevail over us, we should think, "What am I, a Christian or a heathen? Baptized or not baptized? If a Christian, if baptized, shall I rank myself with Gentiles, and join with them in their pursuits?" <div eID="gen25909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25910" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is needless for them to disquiet themselves with care about the necessary supports of life; for they have a Father in heaven who does and will take care for them: "<hi type="italic">Your Father knows that you have need of these things,</hi> and considers it, and will supply your needs <hi type="italic">according to his riches in glory;</hi> for he is <hi type="italic">your Father,</hi> who <hi type="italic">made</hi> you subject to these necessities, and therefore will suit his compassions to them: <hi type="italic">your Father,</hi> who <hi type="italic">maintains</hi> you, educates you, and designs an inheritance for you, and therefore will take care that you <hi type="italic">want no good thing.</hi>" <div eID="gen25910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25911" type="x-p"/> (3.) They have better things to mind and pursue (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.31">v. 31</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But rather seek ye the kingdom of God,</hi> and mind this, you, my disciples, who are to <hi type="italic">preach the kingdom of God;</hi> let your hearts be upon your work, and your great care how to do that well, and this will effectually divert your thoughts from inordinate care about things of the world. And let all that have souls to save <hi type="italic">seek the kingdom of God,</hi> in which only they can be <hi type="italic">safe.</hi> Seek admission into it, seek advancement in it; seek the <hi type="italic">kingdom of grace,</hi> to be subjects in that; the <hi type="italic">kingdom of glory,</hi> to be princes in that; and then <hi type="italic">all these things shall be added to you.</hi> Mind the affairs of your souls with diligence and care, and then trust God with all your other affairs." <div eID="gen25911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25912" type="x-p"/> (4.) They have better things to expect and hope for: <hi type="italic">Fear not, little flock,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.32">v. 32</reference>. For the banishing of inordinate cares, it is necessary that fears should be suppressed. When we frighten ourselves with an apprehension of evil to come, we put ourselves upon the stretch of care how to avoid it, when after all perhaps it is but the creature of our own imagination. Therefore <hi type="italic">fear not, little flock,</hi> but <hi type="italic">hope to the end;</hi> for <hi type="italic">it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.</hi> This comfortable word we had not in Matthew. Note, [1.] Christ's flock in this world is a <hi type="italic">little flock;</hi> his sheep are but few and feeble. The church is a vineyard, a garden, a small spot, compared with the wilderness of this world; as Israel (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.27">1 Kings xx. 27</reference>), who were like two little flocks of kids, when <hi type="italic">the Syrians filled the country.</hi> [2.] Though it be a little flock, quite <hi type="italic">over-numbered,</hi> and therefore in danger of being <hi type="italic">overpowered,</hi> by its enemies, yet it is the will of Christ that they should not <hi type="italic">be afraid: "Fear not, little flock,</hi> but see yourselves safe under the protection and conduct of the great and good Shepherd, and lie easy." [3.] God has <hi type="italic">a kingdom</hi> in store for all that belong to Christ's <hi type="italic">little flock,</hi> a crown of glory (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1 Pet. v. 4</reference>), a throne of power (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev. iii. 21</reference>), unsearchable riches, far exceeding the peculiar treasures of <hi type="italic">kings and provinces.</hi> The <hi type="italic">sheep on the right hand</hi> are called to <hi type="italic">come</hi> and <hi type="italic">inherit the kingdom;</hi> it is theirs for ever; a kingdom for each. [4.] The kingdom is given according to the <hi type="italic">good pleasure</hi> of the Father; <hi type="italic">It is your Father's good pleasure;</hi> it is given not of debt, but of grace, free grace, sovereign grace; <hi type="italic">even so, Father, because it seemed good unto thee.</hi> The kingdom is his; and may he not do what he will with his own? [5.] The believing hopes and prospects of <hi type="italic">the kingdom</hi> should silence and suppress the fears of Christ's little flock in this world. "Fear no trouble; for, though it should come, it shall not come between you and the kingdom, that is sure, it is near." (That is not an evil worth trembling at the thought of which cannot separate us from the love of God). "<hi type="italic">Fear not the want of any</hi> thing that is good for you; for, if it be <hi type="italic">your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom,</hi> you need not question but he will <hi type="italic">bear your charges</hi> thither." <div eID="gen25912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25913" type="x-p"/> II. He charged them to make sure work for their souls, by laying up their treasure in heaven, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.33-Luke.12.34">v. 33, 34</reference>. Those who have done this may be very easy as to all the events of time. <div eID="gen25913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25914" type="x-p"/> 1. "<hi type="italic">Sit loose to this world,</hi> and to all your possessions in it: <hi type="italic">Sell that ye have,</hi> and <hi type="italic">give alms,</hi>" that is, "rather than want wherewith to relieve those that are truly <hi type="italic">necessitous,</hi> sell what you have that is <hi type="italic">superfluous,</hi> all that you can spare from the support of yourselves and families, and give it <hi type="italic">to the poor. Sell what you have,</hi> if you find it a hindrance from, or incumbrance in, the service of Christ. Do not think yourselves undone, if by being fined, imprisoned, or banished, for the testimony of Jesus, you be forced to sell your estates, thought they be <hi type="italic">the inheritance of your fathers.</hi> Do not sell to <hi type="italic">hoard up</hi> the money, or because you can make more of it by usury, but <hi type="italic">sell and give alms;</hi> what is given in alms, in a right manner, is put out to the <hi type="italic">best</hi> interest, upon the <hi type="italic">best</hi> security." <div eID="gen25914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25915" type="x-p"/> 2. "<hi type="italic">Set your hearts upon the other world,</hi> and your expectations from that world. <hi type="italic">Provide yourselves bags that wax not old,</hi> that wax not empty, not of gold, but of grace in the heart and good works in the life; these are the bags that will last." Grace will <hi type="italic">go with us</hi> into another world, for it is <hi type="italic">woven in</hi> the soul; and our good works will <hi type="italic">follow us,</hi> for <hi type="italic">God is not unrighteous to forget</hi> them. These will be <hi type="italic">treasures in heaven,</hi> that will enrich us to eternity. (1.) It is treasure that will not be <hi type="italic">exhausted;</hi> we may spend upon it to eternity, and it will not be at all the less; there is no danger of seeing the bottom of it. (2.) It is treasure that we are in no danger of being robbed of, for <hi type="italic">no thief approaches</hi> near it; what is laid up in heaven is out of reach of enemies. (3.) It is treasure that will not <hi type="italic">spoil</hi> with <hi type="italic">keeping,</hi> any more than it will <hi type="italic">waste</hi> with <hi type="italic">spending;</hi> the <hi type="italic">moth</hi> does not <hi type="italic">corrupt</hi> it, as it does our garments which we now wear. Now by <hi type="italic">this</hi> it appears that we have laid up our treasure in heaven if our <hi type="italic">hearts</hi> be <hi type="italic">there</hi> while we are <hi type="italic">here</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.34">v. 34</reference>), if we think much of heaven and keep our eye upon it, if we quicken ourselves with the hopes of it and keep ourselves in awe with the fear of falling short of it. But, if your hearts be set upon the earth and the things of it, it is to be feared that you have your treasure and portion in it, and are undone when you leave it. <div eID="gen25915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25916" type="x-p"/> III. He charges them to get ready, and to keep in a readiness for Christ's coming, when all those who have laid up their treasure in heaven shall enter upon the enjoyment of it, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.35">v. 35</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen25916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25917" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ is our <hi type="italic">Master,</hi> and we are his <hi type="italic">servants,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">working</hi> servants, but <hi type="italic">waiting</hi> servants, servants that are to do him honour, in <hi type="italic">waiting</hi> on him, and attending his motions: <hi type="italic">If any man serve me, let him follow me. Follow the Lamb whithersoever he goes.</hi> But that is not all: they must do him honour in <hi type="italic">waiting for him,</hi> and expecting his return. We must be as men that <hi type="italic">wait for their Lord,</hi> that sit up late while he stays out late, to be ready to receive him. <div eID="gen25917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25918" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ our Master, though now <hi type="italic">gone from us,</hi> will <hi type="italic">return again,</hi> return <hi type="italic">from the wedding,</hi> from <hi type="italic">solemnizing</hi> the nuptials abroad, to <hi type="italic">complete</hi> them at home. Christ's servants are now in a state of expectation, <hi type="italic">looking for their Master's glorious appearing,</hi> and doing every thing with an eye to <hi type="italic">that,</hi> and in order to <hi type="italic">that.</hi> He <hi type="italic">will come</hi> to take cognizance of his servants, and, that being a <hi type="italic">critical day,</hi> they shall either stay with him or be turned out of doors, according as they are found in that day. <div eID="gen25918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25919" type="x-p"/> 3. The time of our Master's return is uncertain; it will be <hi type="italic">in the night,</hi> it will be <hi type="italic">far</hi> in the night, when he has long <hi type="italic">deferred</hi> his coming, and when many have done looking for him; in the <hi type="italic">second watch,</hi> just before midnight, or in the <hi type="italic">third watch,</hi> next after midnight, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.38">v. 38</reference>. His coming to us, at our death, is uncertain, and to many it will be a great surprise; for <hi type="italic">the Son of Man cometh at an hour that ye think not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.40">v. 40</reference>), without giving notice beforehand. This bespeaks not only the uncertainty of the time of his coming, but the prevailing security of the greatest part of men, who are <hi type="italic">unthinking,</hi> and altogether regardless of the notices given them, so that, whenever he comes, it is <hi type="italic">in an hour that they think not.</hi> <div eID="gen25919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25920" type="x-p"/> 4. That which he expects and requires from his servants is that they be <hi type="italic">ready to open to him immediately,</hi> whenever he comes (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.36">v. 36</reference>), that is, that they be in a frame fit to receive him, or rather to be received by him; that they be found <hi type="italic">as</hi> his servants, in the posture that becomes them, with their <hi type="italic">loins girded about,</hi> alluding to the servants that are ready to go whither their master sends them, and do what their master bids them, having their long garments tucked up (which otherwise would hang about them, and hinder them), and <hi type="italic">their lights burning,</hi> with which to light their master into the house, and up to his chamber. <div eID="gen25920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25921" type="x-p"/> 5. Those servants will be happy who shall be found ready, and in a good frame, when their Lord shall come (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed are those servants</hi> who, after having waited long, continue in a waiting frame, until the hour that their Lord comes, and are then found awake and aware of his first approach, of his first knock; and again (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed are those servants,</hi> for then will be the time of their preferment. Here is such an instance of honour done them as is scarcely to be found among men: He <hi type="italic">will make them sit down to meat, and will serve them.</hi> For the bridegroom to wait upon his bride at table is not uncommon, but to wait upon his servants is not <hi type="italic">the manner of men;</hi> yet Jesus Christ was among his disciples as <hi type="italic">one that served,</hi> and did once, to show his condescension, <hi type="italic">gird himself,</hi> and <hi type="italic">serve them,</hi> when he <hi type="italic">washed their feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.13.4-John.13.5">John xiii. 4, 5</reference>); it signified the joy with which they shall be received into the other world by the Lord Jesus, who is gone before, to prepare for them, and has told them that his <hi type="italic">Father</hi> will <hi type="italic">honour</hi> them, <reference osisRef="John.12.26">John xii. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen25921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25922" type="x-p"/> 6. We are <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> kept at uncertainty concerning the precise time of his coming that we may be always ready; for it is no thanks to a man to be ready for an attack, if he know beforehand just the time when it will be made: <hi type="italic">The good man of the house, if he had known what hour the thief would have come,</hi> though he were ever so careless a man, <hi type="italic">would</hi> yet <hi type="italic">have watched,</hi> and have frightened away the thieves, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.39">v. 39</reference>. But we do not know at what hour the alarm will be given us, and therefore are concerned to watch at all tines, and never to be off our guard. Or this may intimate the miserable case of those who are careless and unbelieving in this great matter. If the <hi type="italic">good man of the house</hi> had had notice of his danger of being robbed such a night, he would have sat up, and saved his house; but we have notice of the day of the Lord's coming, <hi type="italic">as a thief in the night,</hi> to the confusion and ruin of all secure sinners, and yet do not thus <hi type="italic">watch.</hi> If men will take such care of their houses, O let us be thus wise for our souls: <hi type="italic">Be ye therefore ready also,</hi> as ready as the good man of the house would be <hi type="italic">if he knew what hour the thief would come.</hi>
