entries.08294e95cb9ce1d6832c35d159ca2ca964a54f8b: <div eID="gen25922" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Vigilance and Exertion Inculcated.</title> <div sID="gen25923" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> Then Peter said unto him, Lord, speakest thou this parable unto us, or even to all? <hi type="super">42</hi> And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom <hi type="italic">his</hi> lord shall make ruler over his household, to give <hi type="italic">them their</hi> portion of meat in due season? <hi type="super">43</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing. <hi type="super">44</hi> Of a truth I say unto you, that he will make him ruler over all that he hath. <hi type="super">45</hi> But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken; 46 The lord of that servant will come in a day when he looketh not for <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and at a hour when he is not aware, and will cut him in sunder, and will appoint him his portion with the unbelievers. <hi type="super">47</hi> And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many <hi type="italic">stripes.</hi> <hi type="super">48</hi> But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few <hi type="italic">stripes.</hi> For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more. <hi type="super">49</hi> I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled? <hi type="super">50</hi> But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished! <hi type="super">51</hi> Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division: <hi type="super">52</hi> For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three. <hi type="super">53</hi> The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother in law against her daughter in law, and the daughter in law against her mother in law. <div eID="gen25923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25924" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Peter's question, which he put to Christ upon occasion of the foregoing parable (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.41">v. 41</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, speakest thou this parable to us</hi> that are thy constant followers, to us that are ministers, <hi type="italic">or also to all</hi> that come to be taught by thee, to all the hearers, and in them to all Christians?" Peter was now, as often, spokesman for the disciples. We have reason to bless God that there are some such forward men, that have a gift of utterance; let those that are such take heed of being proud. Now Peter desires Christ to explain himself, and to direct the arrow of the foregoing parable to the mark he intended. He calls it a <hi type="italic">parable,</hi> because it was not only figurative, but weighty, solid, and instructive. Lord, said Peter, was it intended for <hi type="italic">us,</hi> or for <hi type="italic">all?</hi> To this Christ gives a direct answer (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.37">Mark xiii. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">What I say unto you, I say unto all.</hi> Yet here he seems to show that the apostles were primarily concerned in it. Note, We are all concerned to take to ourselves what Christ in his word designs for us, and to enquire accordingly concerning it: <hi type="italic">Speakest thou this to us?</hi> To me? Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears. Doth this word belong to me? Speak it to <hi type="italic">my heart.</hi> <div eID="gen25924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25925" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's reply to this question, directed to Peter and the rest of the disciples. If what Christ had said before did not so peculiarly concern them, but in common with other Christians, who must all watch and pray for Christ's coming, <hi type="italic">as his servants,</hi> yet this that follows is peculiarly adapted to ministers, who are the <hi type="italic">stewards</hi> in Christ's house. Now our Lord Jesus here tells them, <div eID="gen25925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25926" type="x-p"/> 1. What was their <hi type="italic">duty as stewards,</hi> and what the <hi type="italic">trust</hi> committed to them. (1.) They are made <hi type="italic">rulers of God's household,</hi> under Christ, whose own the house is; ministers derive an authority from Christ to preach the gospel, and to administer the ordinances of Christ, and apply the seals of the covenant of grace. (2.) Their business is to give God's children and servants <hi type="italic">their portion of meat,</hi> that which is proper for them and allotted to them; convictions and comfort to those to whom they respectively belong. <hi type="italic">Suum cuique</hi>—<hi type="italic">to every one his own.</hi> This is <hi type="italic">rightly to divide the word of truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.15">2 Tim. ii. 15</reference>. (3.) To give it to them <hi type="italic">in due season,</hi> at that time and in that way which are most suitable to the temper and condition of those that are to be fed; a word <hi type="italic">in season</hi> to him <hi type="italic">that is weary.</hi> (4.) Herein they must approve themselves <hi type="italic">faithful</hi> and <hi type="italic">wise; faithful</hi> to their Master, by whom this great trust is reposed in them, and faithful to their fellow-servants, for whose benefit they are put in trust; and <hi type="italic">wise</hi> to improve an opportunity of doing honour to their Master, and service in the family. Ministers must be both <hi type="italic">skilful</hi> and <hi type="italic">faithful.</hi> <div eID="gen25926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25927" type="x-p"/> 2. What would be their happiness if they approved themselves faithful and wise (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed is that servant,</hi> (1.) That is <hi type="italic">doing,</hi> and is not idle, nor indulgent of his ease; even the rulers of the household must be <hi type="italic">doing,</hi> and make themselves <hi type="italic">servants of all.</hi> (2.) That is <hi type="italic">so</hi> doing, doing as he should be, giving them their <hi type="italic">portion of meat,</hi> by public preaching and personal application. (3.) That is <hi type="italic">found</hi> so doing when his Lord comes; that perseveres to the end, notwithstanding the difficulties he may meet with in the way. Now his happiness is illustrated by the preferment of a steward that has approved himself within a lower and narrower degree of service; he shall be preferred to a larger and higher (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.44">v. 44</reference>): <hi type="italic">He will make him ruler over all that he has,</hi> which was Joseph's preferment in Pharaoh's court. Note, Ministers that obtain mercy of the Lord to be faithful shall obtain further mercy to be abundantly rewarded for their faithfulness in the day of the Lord. <div eID="gen25927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25928" type="x-p"/> 3. What a dreadful reckoning there would be if they were treacherous and unfaithful, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.45-Luke.12.46">v. 45, 46</reference>. If that servant begin to be quarrelsome and profane, he shall be called to an account, and severely punished. We had all this before in Matthew, and therefore shall here only observe, (1.) Our looking upon Christ's second coming as a thing at a distance is the cause of all those irregularities which render the thought of it terrible to us: <hi type="italic">He saith in his heart, My Lord delays his coming.</hi> Christ's patience is very often misinterpreted his <hi type="italic">delay,</hi> to the <hi type="italic">dis</hi>couragement of his people, and the <hi type="italic">en</hi>couragement of his enemies. (2.) The persecutors of God's people are commonly abandoned to security and sensuality; <hi type="italic">they beat their fellow-servants,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">eat and drink with the drunken,</hi> altogether unconcerned either at their own sin or their brethren's sufferings, as the king and Haman, who <hi type="italic">sat down to drink when the city Shushan was perplexed.</hi> Thus they drink, to drown the clamours of their own consciences, and baffle them, which would otherwise fly in their faces. (3.) Death and judgment will be very terrible to all wicked people, but especially to wicked ministers. It will be a surprise to them: <hi type="italic">At an hour when they are not aware.</hi> It will be the determining of them to endless misery; they shall be cut in sunder, and have their portion assigned them with <hi type="italic">the unbelievers.</hi> <div eID="gen25928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25929" type="x-p"/> 4. What an aggravation it would be of their sin and punishment that they knew their duty, and did not do it (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.47-Luke.12.48">v. 47, 48</reference>): <hi type="italic">That servant that knew his lord's will, and did it not, shall be beaten with many stripes,</hi> shall fall under a sorer punishment; and <hi type="italic">he that knew not shall be beaten with few stripes,</hi> his punishment shall, in consideration of this, be mitigated. Here seems to be an allusion to the law, which made a distinction between sins committed through ignorance, and presumptuous sins (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.15 Num.15.29-Num.15.30">Lev. v. 15, &c.; Num. xv. 29, 30</reference>), as also to another law concerning the number of stripes given to a malefactor, to be according to the nature of the crime, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.2-Deut.25.3">Deut. xxv. 2, 3</reference>. Now, (1.) Ignorance of our duty is an extenuation of sin. He <hi type="italic">that knew not his lord's will,</hi> through carelessness and neglect, and his not having such opportunities as some others had of coming to the knowledge of it, and <hi type="italic">did things worthy of stripes,</hi> he shall <hi type="italic">be beaten,</hi> because he might have known his duty better, but <hi type="italic">with few stripes;</hi> his ignorance excuses in part, but not wholly. Thus <hi type="italic">through ignorance</hi> the Jews put Christ to death (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.17">Acts iii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>), and Christ pleaded that ignorance in their excuse: <hi type="italic">They know not what they do.</hi> (2.) The knowledge of our duty is an aggravation of our sin: <hi type="italic">That servant that knew his lord's will,</hi> and yet did his own will, shall be <hi type="italic">beaten with many stripes.</hi> God will justly inflict more upon him for abusing the means of knowledge he afforded him, which others would have made a better use of, because it argues a great degree of wilfulness and contempt to sin against knowledge; of how much sorer punishment then shall they be thought worthy, besides the many stripes that their own consciences will give them! Son, remember. Here is a good reason for this added: <hi type="italic">To whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required,</hi> especially when it is <hi type="italic">committed</hi> as a trust he is to account for. Those have greater capacities of mind than others, more knowledge and learning, more acquaintance and converse with the scriptures, to them <hi type="italic">much is given,</hi> and their account will be accordingly. <div eID="gen25929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25930" type="x-p"/> III. A further discourse concerning his own sufferings, which he expected, and concerning the sufferings of his followers, which he would have them also to live in expectation of. In general (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am come to send fire on the earth.</hi> By this some understand the preaching of the gospel, and the pouring out of the Spirit, holy fire; this Christ came to send with a commission to refine the world, to purge away its dross, to burn up its chaff, and it was <hi type="italic">already kindled.</hi> The gospel was begun to be preached; some prefaces there were to the pouring out of the Spirit. Christ baptized with the Holy Ghost and with fire; this Spirit descended in fiery tongues. But, by what follows, it seems rather to be understood of the fire of <hi type="italic">persecution.</hi> Christ is not the Author of it, as it is the sin of the incendiaries, the <hi type="italic">persecutors;</hi> but he <hi type="italic">permits</hi> it, nay, he <hi type="italic">commissions</hi> it, as a <hi type="italic">refining</hi> fire for the <hi type="italic">trial</hi> of the <hi type="italic">persecuted.</hi> This fire was <hi type="italic">already kindled</hi> in the enmity of the carnal Jews to Christ and his followers. "<hi type="italic">What will I that it may presently be kindled? What thou doest, do quickly. If it be already kindled, what will I?</hi> Shall I wait the <hi type="italic">quenching</hi> of it? No, for it must fasten upon myself, and upon all, and glory will redound to God from it." <div eID="gen25930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25931" type="x-p"/> 1. He must himself suffer many things; he must pass through this fire that was already kindled (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.50">v. 50</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have a baptism to be baptized with.</hi> Afflictions are compared both to <hi type="italic">fire</hi> and <hi type="italic">water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Ps. lxvi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.2">lxix. 1, 2</reference>. Christ's sufferings were both. He calls them a <hi type="italic">baptism</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.22">Matt. xx. 22</reference>); for he was watered or sprinkled with them, as Israel was baptized <hi type="italic">in the cloud,</hi> and dipped into them, as Israel was baptized <hi type="italic">in the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.2">1 Cor. x. 2</reference>. He must be sprinkled with his own blood, and with the blood of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">Isa. lxiii. 3</reference>. See here, (1.) Christ's <hi type="italic">foresight</hi> of his sufferings; he knew what he was to undergo, and the necessity of undergoing it: <hi type="italic">I am to be baptized with a baptism.</hi> He calls his sufferings by a name that <hi type="italic">mitigates</hi> them; it is a baptism, not a deluge; I must be <hi type="italic">dipped</hi> in them, not <hi type="italic">drowned</hi> in them; and by a name that <hi type="italic">sanctifies</hi> them, for baptism is a name that <hi type="italic">sanctifies</hi> them, for baptism is a sacred rite. Christ in his sufferings <hi type="italic">devoted</hi> himself to his Father's honour, and <hi type="italic">consecrated</hi> himself a priest for evermore, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.27-Heb.7.28">Heb. vii. 27, 28</reference>. (2.) Christ's <hi type="italic">forwardness</hi> to his sufferings: <hi type="italic">How am I straitened till it be accomplished!</hi> He longed for the time when he should suffer and die, having an eye to the glorious issue of his sufferings. It is an allusion to a woman in travail, that is <hi type="italic">pained to be delivered,</hi> and welcomes her pains, because they hasten the birth of the child, and wishes them sharp and strong, that the <hi type="italic">work</hi> may be <hi type="italic">cut short.</hi> Christ's sufferings were the <hi type="italic">travail of his soul,</hi> which he cheerfully underwent, in hope that he should by them <hi type="italic">see his seed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10-Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 10, 11</reference>. So much was his heart set upon the redemption and salvation of man. <div eID="gen25931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25932" type="x-p"/> 2. He tells those about him that they also must bear with hardships and difficulties (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.51">v. 51</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Suppose ye that I came to give peace on earth,</hi> to give you a peaceable possession of the earth, and outward prosperity on the earth?" It is intimated that they were ready to entertain such a thought as this, nay, that they went upon this supposition, that the gospel would meet with a <hi type="italic">universal</hi> welcome, that people <hi type="italic">unanimously</hi> embrace it, and would therefore study to make the preachers of it <hi type="italic">easy</hi> and <hi type="italic">great,</hi> that Christ, if he did not give them <hi type="italic">pomp</hi> and <hi type="italic">power,</hi> would at least give them <hi type="italic">peace;</hi> and herein they were encouraged by divers passages of the Old Testament, which speak of the peace of the Messiah's kingdom, which they were willing to understand of external peace. "But," saith Christ, "you will be mistaken, the event will declare the contrary, and therefore do not flatter yourselves into a fool's paradise. You will find," <div eID="gen25932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25933" type="x-p"/> (1.) "That the effect of the preaching of the gospel will be <hi type="italic">division.</hi>" Not but that the design of the gospel and its proper tendency are to unite the children of men to one another, to knit them together in holy love, and, if all would receive it, this would be the effect of it; but there being multitudes that not only will not receive it, but oppose it, and have their corruptions exasperated by it, and are enraged at those that do receive it, it proves, though not the <hi type="italic">cause</hi> yet the <hi type="italic">occasion</hi> of <hi type="italic">division.</hi> While <hi type="italic">the strong man armed kept his palace,</hi> in the Gentile world, <hi type="italic">his goods were at peace;</hi> all was quiet, for all went one way, the sects of philosophers agreed well enough, so did the worshippers of different deities; but when the gospel was preached, and many were enlightened by it, and turned from the power of Satan to God, then there was a disturbance, <hi type="italic">a noise and a shaking,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.7">Ezek. xxxvii. 7</reference>. Some <hi type="italic">distinguished</hi> themselves by embracing the gospel, and others were angry that they did so. Yea, and among them that received the gospel there would be different sentiments in minor things, which would occasion <hi type="italic">division;</hi> and Christ permits it for holy ends (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.18">1 Cor. xi. 18</reference>), that Christians may learn and practise mutual forbearance, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.1-Rom.14.2">Rom. xiv. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen25933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25934" type="x-p"/> (2.) "That this <hi type="italic">division</hi> will reach into private families, and the preaching of the gospel will give occasion for discord among the nearest relations" (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.53">v. 53</reference>): <hi type="italic">The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father,</hi> when the one turns Christian and the other does not; for the one that does turn Christian will be zealous by arguments and endearments to turn the other too, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.16">1 Cor. vii. 16</reference>. As soon as ever Paul was converted, he <hi type="italic">disputed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.29">Acts ix. 29</reference>. The one that continues in unbelief will be provoked, and will hate and persecute the one that by his faith and obedience witnesses against, and condemns, his unbelief and disobedience. A spirit of bigotry and persecution will break through the strongest bonds of relation and natural affection; see <reference osisRef="Matt.10.35">Matt. x. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">xxiv. 7</reference>. Even <hi type="italic">mothers</hi> and <hi type="italic">daughters</hi> fall out about religion; and those that believe not are so violent and outrageous that they are ready to deliver up into the hands of the bloody persecutors those that believe, though otherwise very near and dear to them. We find in the <hi type="italic">Acts</hi> that, wherever the gospel came, <hi type="italic">persecution</hi> was <hi type="italic">stirred up;</hi> it was <hi type="italic">every where spoken against,</hi> and there was <hi type="italic">no small stir about that way.</hi> Therefore let not the disciples of Christ promise themselves <hi type="italic">peace upon earth,</hi> for they are sent forth <hi type="italic">as sheep in the midst of wolves.</hi>
entries.980b89baf4327cecfb772f99637e64175394197b: <div eID="gen25934" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Reconciliation to God.</title> <div sID="gen25935" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">54</hi> And he said also to the people, When ye see a cloud rise out of the west, straightway ye say, There cometh a shower; and so it is. <hi type="super">55</hi> And when <hi type="italic">ye see</hi> the south wind blow, ye say, There will be heat; and it cometh to pass. 56 <hi type="italic">Ye</hi> hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky and of the earth; but how is it that ye do not discern this time? 57 Yea, and why even of yourselves judge ye not what is right? <hi type="super">58</hi> When thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate, <hi type="italic">as thou art</hi> in the way, give diligence that thou mayest be delivered from him; lest he hale thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and the officer cast thee into prison. <hi type="super">59</hi> I tell thee, thou shalt not depart thence, till thou hast paid the very last mite. <div eID="gen25935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25936" type="x-p"/> Having given his disciples <hi type="italic">their</hi> lesson in the foregoing verses, here Christ turns to <hi type="italic">the people,</hi> and gives them <hi type="italic">theirs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.54">v. 54</reference>. He <hi type="italic">said also to the people:</hi> he preached <hi type="italic">ad populum—to the people,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">ad clerum—to the clergy.</hi> In general, he would have them be as wise in the affairs of their souls as they are in their outward affairs. Two things he specifies:— <div eID="gen25936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25937" type="x-p"/> I. Let them learn to <hi type="italic">discern the way of God towards them,</hi> that they may <hi type="italic">prepare</hi> accordingly. They were <hi type="italic">weather-wise,</hi> and by observing the winds and clouds could foresee when there would be <hi type="italic">rain</hi> and when there would be <hi type="italic">hot weather</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.54-Luke.12.55">v. 54, 55</reference>); and, according as they foresaw the weather would be, they either housed their hay and corn, or threw it abroad, and equipped themselves for a journey? Even in regard to changes of the weather God gives warning to us what is coming, and art has improved the notices of nature in weather-glasses. The prognostications here referred to had their origin in repeated observations upon the chain of causes: from what <hi type="italic">has been</hi> we conjecture what <hi type="italic">will be.</hi> See the benefit of experience; by <hi type="italic">taking notice</hi> we may come to <hi type="italic">give notice.</hi> Whose is wise will <hi type="italic">observe</hi> and <hi type="italic">learn.</hi> See now. <div eID="gen25937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25938" type="x-p"/> 1. The particulars of the presages: "<hi type="italic">When you see a cloud arising out of the west</hi>" (the Hebrew would say, <hi type="italic">out of the sea</hi>), "perhaps it is at first <hi type="italic">no bigger than a man's hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.44">1 Kings xviii. 44</reference>), but you say, There is a shower in the womb of it, and it proves so. When you <hi type="italic">observe</hi> the <hi type="italic">south wind blow,</hi> you say, <hi type="italic">There will be heat</hi>" (for the hot countries of Africa lay not far south from Judea), "and it usually <hi type="italic">comes to pass;</hi>" yet nature has not ties itself to such a track but that <hi type="italic">sometimes</hi> we are mistaken in our prognostics. <div eID="gen25938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25939" type="x-p"/> 2. The inferences from them (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.56">v. 56</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Ye hypocrites,</hi> who pretend to be wise, but really are not so, who pretend to expect the Messiah and his kingdom" (for so the generality of the Jews did) "and yet are no way disposed to receive and entertain it, <hi type="italic">how is it that you do not discern this time,</hi> that you do not discern that now is the time, according to the indications given in the Old-Testament prophecies, for the Messiah to appear, and that, according to the marks given of him, I am he? Why are you not aware that you have now an opportunity which you <hi type="italic">will not have long,</hi> and which you <hi type="italic">may never have again,</hi> of securing to yourselves an interest in the kingdom of God and the privileges of that kingdom?" <hi type="italic">Now is the accepted time,</hi> now or never. It is the folly and misery of man that he <hi type="italic">knows not his time,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Eccl. ix. 12</reference>. This was the ruin of the men of that generation, that they <hi type="italic">knew not the day of their visitation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.44">ch. xix. 44</reference>. But a <hi type="italic">wise man's heart discerns time and judgment;</hi> such was the wisdom of the men of Issachar, who <hi type="italic">had understanding of the times,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.32">1 Chron. xii. 32</reference>. He adds, "<hi type="italic">Yea, and why even of yourselves,</hi> though ye had not these loud alarms given you, <hi type="italic">judge ye not what is right?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.57">v. 57</reference>. You are not only stupid and regardless in matters that are purely of divine revelation, and take not the hints which that gives you, but you are so even in the dictates of the very light and law of nature." Christianity has reason and natural conscience on its side; and, if men would allow themselves the liberty of <hi type="italic">judging what is right,</hi> they would soon find that all Christ's precepts concerning all things are right, and that there is nothing more equitable in itself, nor better becoming us, than to submit to them and be ruled by them. <div eID="gen25939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25940" type="x-p"/> II. Let them hasten to <hi type="italic">make their peace with God</hi> in time, before it be too late, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.58-Luke.12.59">v. 58, 59</reference>. This we had upon another occasion, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.25-Matt.5.26">Matt. v. 25, 26</reference>. 1. We reckon it our wisdom in our temporal affairs to <hi type="italic">compound</hi> with those with whom we cannot <hi type="italic">contend,</hi> to <hi type="italic">agree with our adversary</hi> upon the best terms we can, before the equity be <hi type="italic">foreclosed,</hi> and we be left to the rigour of the law: "<hi type="italic">When thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate,</hi> to whom the appeal is made, and knowest that he has an advantage against thee, and thou art in danger of being cast, thou knowest it is the most prudent course to make the matter up between yourselves; <hi type="italic">as thou art in the way, give diligence to be delivered from him,</hi> to get a discharge, lest judgment be given, and execution awarded according to law." Wise men will not let their quarrels go to an extremity, but accommodate them in time. 2. Let us do thus in the affairs of our souls. We have by sin made God our <hi type="italic">adversary,</hi> have provoked his displeasure against us, and he has both <hi type="italic">right</hi> and <hi type="italic">might</hi> on his side; so that it is to no purpose to think of carrying on the controversy with him either at <hi type="italic">bar</hi> or in <hi type="italic">battle.</hi> Christ, to whom all judgment is committed, is the magistrate before whom we are hastening to appear: if we stand a trial before him, and insist upon our own justification, the cause will certainly go against us, the <hi type="italic">Judge</hi> will <hi type="italic">deliver</hi> us to the <hi type="italic">officer,</hi> the ministers of his justice, and we shall be <hi type="italic">cast into</hi> the <hi type="italic">prison</hi> of hell, and the debt will be exacted to the utmost; though we cannot make a full satisfaction for it, it will be continually demanded, <hi type="italic">till the last mite be paid,</hi> which will not be to all eternity. Christ's sufferings were short, yet the <hi type="italic">value</hi> of them made them fully satisfactory. In the sufferings of damned sinners what is wanting in value must be made up in an endless duration. Now, in consideration of this, let us give diligence to be delivered <hi type="italic">out of</hi> the hands of God as an adversary, into his hands as a Father, and this <hi type="italic">as we are in the way,</hi> which has the chief stress laid upon it here. While we are alive, we are <hi type="italic">in the way;</hi> and <hi type="italic">now</hi> is our <hi type="italic">time,</hi> by repentance and faith through Christ (who is the Mediator as well as the magistrate), to get the quarrel made up, while it may be done, before it be too late. Thus was God in Christ <hi type="italic">reconciling the world to himself, beseeching us to be reconciled.</hi> Let us take hold on the arm of the Lord stretched out in this gracious offer, that we may make peace, and we <hi type="italic">shall make peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.4-Isa.27.5">Isa. xxvii. 4, 5</reference>), for we cannot <hi type="italic">walk together</hi> till we be <hi type="italic">agreed.</hi>  <chapter eID="Luke.12"/> <div eID="gen25940" type="x-p"/>

entries.f79b82eaf1af8826febd031428a671df1e7565c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14494"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.12.1-Luke.12.12">Lu 12:1-12</reference>. Warning against Hypocrisy.</title> <div sID="gen28050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14494"/><hi type="bold">1-3. meantime--</hi>in close connection, probably, with the foregoing scene. Our Lord had been speaking out more plainly than ever before, as matters were coming to a head between Him and His enemies, and this seems to have suggested to His own mind the warning here. He had just Himself illustriously exemplified His own precepts.<div eID="gen28050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his disciples first of all--</hi>afterwards to "the multitudes" (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.54">Lu 12:54</reference>).<div eID="gen28051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covered--</hi>from the view. <div eID="gen28052" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4ed064e9ece3188b240ee178da46e16111d92e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14496"/><div sID="gen28054" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14496"/><hi type="bold">4-5. I say, &c.--</hi>You will say, That may cost us our life. Be it so; but, "My friends, there their power ends." He calls them "my friends" here, not in any loose sense, but, as we think, from the feeling He then had that in this "killing of the body" He and they were going to be affectingly one with each other. <div eID="gen28054" type="x-p"/>
entries.25eda3dd3219d29dc9e33d3124e1810191aadec9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14498"/><div sID="gen28057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14498"/><hi type="bold">6-7. five ... for two farthings--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Matt.10.29">Mt 10:29</reference> it is "two for one farthing"; so if one took two farthings' worth, he got one in addition--of such small value were they.<div eID="gen28057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">than many sparrows--</hi>not "than millions of sparrows"; the charm and power of our Lord's teaching is very much in this simplicity. <div eID="gen28058" type="x-p"/>
entries.adb6a4cddd38fb27301233c9ccac4b952e8e3b6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14499"/><div sID="gen28059" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14499"/><hi type="bold">8-9. confess ... deny--</hi>The point lies in doing it "before men," because one has to do it "despising the shame." But when done, the Lord holds Himself bound to repay it in kind by confessing such "before the angels of God." For the rest, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.9.26">Lu 9:26</reference>. <div eID="gen28059" type="x-p"/>
entries.09a252e27f74462f75edae0b1e0b3deca2ccee4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14500"/><div sID="gen28060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14500"/><hi type="bold">10. Son of man ... Holy Ghost--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.31">Mt 12:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.32">32</reference>). <div eID="gen28060" type="x-p"/>
entries.2093c40fb1c24adc12b6364911919bc19dfc5696: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14501"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.12.13-Luke.12.53">Lu 12:13-53</reference>. Covetousness--Watchfulness--Superiority to Earthly Ties.</title> <div sID="gen28061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14501"/><hi type="bold">13. Master, &c.--</hi>that is, "Great Preacher of righteousness, help; there is need of Thee in this rapacious world; here am I the victim of injustice, and that from my own brother, who withholds from me my rightful share of the inheritance that has fallen to us." In this most inopportune intrusion upon the solemnities of our Lord's teaching, there is a mixture of the absurd and the irreverent, the one, however, occasioning the other. The man had not the least idea that his case was not of as urgent a nature, and as worthy the attention of our Lord, as anything else He could deal with. <div eID="gen28061" type="x-p"/>
entries.f67726291842d6a0fb42dc9d992a5b5b34f85be4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14502"/><div sID="gen28062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14502"/><hi type="bold">14. Man, &c.--</hi>Contrast this style of address with "my friends," (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.4">Lu 12:4</reference>).<div eID="gen28062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who, &c.--</hi>a question literally repudiating the office which Moses assumed (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.14">Ex 2:14</reference>). The influence of religious teachers in the external relations of life has ever been immense, when only the INDIRECT effect of their teaching; but whenever they intermeddle DIRECTLY with secular and political matters, the spell of that influence is broken. <div eID="gen28063" type="x-p"/>
entries.af75843cbba6ea72ac49899ab2f5ea31df595254: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14503"/><div sID="gen28064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14503"/><hi type="bold">15. unto them--</hi>the multitude around Him (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.1">Lu 12:1</reference>).<div eID="gen28064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of covetousness--</hi>The best copies have "all," that is, "every kind of covetousness"; because as this was one of the more plausible forms of it, so He would strike at once at the root of the evil.<div eID="gen28065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man's life, &c.--</hi>a singularly weighty maxim, and not less so because its meaning and its truth are equally evident. <div eID="gen28066" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0178508c3818180db619f277a93eda000595bc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14504"/><div sID="gen28067" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14504"/><hi type="bold">16-19. a certain rich man, &c.--</hi>Why is this man called a "fool?" (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Lu 12:20</reference>) (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.1">1</reference>) Because he deemed a life of secure and abundant earthly enjoyment the summit of human felicity. (2) Because, possessing the means of this, through prosperity in his calling, he flattered himself that he had a long lease of such enjoyment, and nothing to do but give himself up to it. Nothing else is laid to his charge. <div eID="gen28067" type="x-p"/>
entries.840eac6ce36cedff7211e650267c0cf021d2d507: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14505"/><div sID="gen28068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14505"/><hi type="bold">20-21. this night, &c.--</hi>This sudden cutting short of his career is designed to express not only the folly of building securely upon the future, but of throwing one's whole soul into what may at any moment be gone. "Thy soul shall be required of thee" is put in opposition to his own treatment of it, "I will say to my soul, Soul," &c.<div eID="gen28068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose shall those things be, &c.--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.39.6">Psa 39:6</reference>, "He heapeth up riches and knoweth not who shall gather them." <div eID="gen28069" type="x-p"/>
entries.08aa709942f388d7aa4f076684c3b9203c813086: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14507"/><div sID="gen28072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14507"/>22-31. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25-Matt.6.33">Mt 6:25-33</reference>). <div eID="gen28072" type="x-p"/>
entries.2446c97ac5946a7205b0ab53599ccd1b6c4ac731: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14510"/><div sID="gen28075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14510"/><hi type="bold">32. little flock, &c.--</hi>How sublime and touching a contrast between this tender and pitying appellation, "Little flock" (in the original a double diminutive, which in German can be expressed, but not in English)--and the "good pleasure" of the Father to give them the Kingdom; the one recalling the insignificance and helplessness of that then literal handful of disciples, the other holding up to their view the eternal love that encircled them, the everlasting arms that were underneath them, and the high inheritance awaiting them!--"the kingdom"; grand word; then why not "bread" (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.31">Lu 12:31</reference> [Bengel]). Well might He say, "Fear not!" <div eID="gen28075" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6977d8da22694f79638d3b88291f8a2c052ff6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14511"/><div sID="gen28076" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14511"/><hi type="bold">33-34. Sell, &c.--</hi>This is but a more vivid expression of <reference osisRef="Matt.6.19-Matt.6.21">Mt 6:19-21</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.6.19-Matt.6.21">Mt 6:19-21</reference>). <div eID="gen28076" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a5a961bde45d61830dd4b3828be625bd2c87840: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14512"/><div sID="gen28077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14512"/><hi type="bold">35-40. loins ... girded--</hi>to fasten up the long outer garment, always done before travel and work (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.29">2Ki 4:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.8">Ac 12:8</reference>). The meaning is, Be in readiness.<div eID="gen28077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lights, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">Mt 25:1</reference>). <div eID="gen28078" type="x-p"/>
entries.e92c72872e2e99ff340ddb5f19ed20f86bbe3abb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14516"/><div sID="gen28082" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14516"/><hi type="bold">41-48. unto us or even to all?--</hi>us the Twelve, or all this vast audience? <div eID="gen28082" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b1219a05e71b305eceb62e007c82eb76897dd05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14522"/><div sID="gen28093" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14522"/><hi type="bold">49-53. to send--</hi>cast.<div eID="gen28093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire--</hi>"the higher spiritual element of life which Jesus came to introduce into this earth (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Mt 3:11</reference>), with reference to its mighty effects in quickening all that is akin to it and destroying all that is opposed. To cause this element of life to take up its abode on earth, and wholly to pervade human hearts with its warmth, was the lofty destiny of the Redeemer" [Olshausen: so Calvin, Stier, Alford, &c.].<div eID="gen28094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28095" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what will I, &c.--</hi>an obscure expression, uttered under deep and half-smothered emotion. In its general import all are agreed; but the nearest to the precise meaning seems to be, "And what should I have to desire if it were once already kindled?" [Bengel and Bloomfield]. <div eID="gen28095" type="x-p"/>
entries.91998be8a7e7c2a41449795a9d03e2efddd97b1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14525"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.12.54-Luke.12.59">Lu 12:54-59</reference>. Not Discerning the Signs of the Time.</title> <div sID="gen28100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14525"/><hi type="bold">54. to the people--</hi>"the multitude," a word of special warning to the thoughtless crowd, before dismissing them. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.16.2">Mt 16:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.3">3</reference>). <div eID="gen28100" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbf652466f2405e39555a30be7bf519ad0fb271f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14526"/><div sID="gen28101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14526"/><hi type="bold">56. how ... not discern, &c.--</hi>unable to perceive what a critical period that was for the Jewish Church. <div eID="gen28101" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ea2393f8153ffab09eaf984f4719aeeedd36f5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14527"/><div sID="gen28102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14527"/><hi type="bold">57. why even of yourselves, &c.--</hi>They might say, To do this requires more knowledge of Scripture and providence than we possess; but He sends them to their own conscience, as enough to show them who He was, and win them to immediate discipleship. <div eID="gen28102" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8cc4dc71175b8af30700ae7f98822a960cdef8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14528"/><div sID="gen28103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14528"/><hi type="bold">58. When thou goest, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.5.25">Mt 5:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.26">26</reference>). The urgency of the case with them, and the necessity, for their own safety, of immediate decision, was the object of these striking words. <chapter eID="Luke.12"/>

entries.311bb41e25d784fed95736d297dd3b3b9f0aab58: <div eID="gen40541" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen40542" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen40543" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen40543" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen40542" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen40544" type="x-p"/> Christ preaches to his disciples against hypocrisy; and against timidity in publishing the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.1-Luk.12.5">Luk 12:1-5</reference>. Excites them to have confidence in Divine providence, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.6">Luk 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.7">Luk 12:7</reference>. Warns them against denying him, or betraying his cause, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.8">Luk 12:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.9">Luk 12:9</reference>. Of the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.10">Luk 12:10</reference>. Promises direction and support in persecution, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.11">Luk 12:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.12">Luk 12:12</reference>. Warns the people against covetousness, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.13-Luk.12.15">Luk 12:13-15</reference>. Parable of the rich man who pulled down his granaries to build greater, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.16-Luk.12.21">Luk 12:16-21</reference>. Cautions against carking cares and anxieties, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.22-Luk.12.32">Luk 12:22-32</reference>. The necessity of living to God, and in reference to eternity, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.33-Luk.12.40">Luk 12:33-40</reference>. At the request of Peter, he farther explains the preceding discourse, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.41-Luk.12.48">Luk 12:41-48</reference>. The effects that should be produced by the preaching of the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.49-Luk.12.53">Luk 12:49-53</reference>. The signs of the times, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.54-Luk.12.57">Luk 12:54-57</reference>. The necessity of being prepared to appear before the judgment seat of God, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.58">Luk 12:58</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.59">Luk 12:59</reference>. <div eID="gen40544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40545" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen40545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40546" type="x-p"/> An innumerable multitude of people - Των μυριαδων του οχλου, myriads of people. A myriad is ten thousand, and myriads must, at the very lowest, mean twenty thousand. But the word is often used to signify a crowd or multitude which cannot be readily numbered. There was doubtless a vast crowd assembled on this occasion, and many of them were deeply instructed by the very important discourse which our Lord delivered. <div eID="gen40546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40547" type="x-p"/> Leaven of the Pharisees - See <reference osisRef="Mat.16.1-Mat.16.12">Mat 16:1-12</reference>. <div eID="gen40547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40548" type="x-p"/> Which is hypocrisy - These words are supposed by some to be an addition to the text, because it does not appear that it is their hypocrisy which Christ alludes to, but their false doctrines. They had, however, a large proportion of both.
entries.25ee9e1c1d77fd541c6193e597835ea93a2cbe4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen40548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40549" type="x-p"/> There is nothing covered - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.5.15">Mat 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.10.26">Mat 10:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.27">Mat 10:27</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mar.4.22">Mar 4:22</reference> (note).
entries.c332b045cae2ab3ae71cc55c55c9b7114724ba2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen40549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40550" type="x-p"/> Kill the body - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.28">Mat 10:28</reference> (note).
entries.7cb19b3ea52d56a515c4496f6c4c7f2eab4aab4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen40550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40551" type="x-p"/> Fear him - Even the friends of God are commanded to fear God, as a being who has authority to send both body and soul into hell. Therefore it is proper even for the most holy persons to maintain a fear of God, as the punisher of all unrighteousness. A man has but one life to lose, and one soul to save; and it is madness to sacrifice the salvation of the soul to the preservation of the life.
entries.988a6633f3a5deb918573b5e80cb4a65c684d4f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen40551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40552" type="x-p"/> Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings? - See this explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.29">Mat 10:29</reference> (note), from which place we learn that two sparrows were sold for one farthing, and here; that five were sold for two farthings: thus we find a certain proportion - for one farthing you could get but two, while for two farthings you could get five.
entries.a7fcc3f0e6f21dda6da511847f422b1fd80f3e9d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen40552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40553" type="x-p"/> Fear not therefore - Want of faith in the providence and goodness of God is the source of all human inquietudes and fears. He has undertaken to save and defend those to the uttermost who trust in him. His wisdom cannot be surprised, his power cannot be forced, his love cannot forget itself. Man distrusts God, and fears that he is forgotten by him, because he judges of God by himself; and he knows that he is apt to forget his Maker, and be unfaithful to him. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.29-Mat.10.31">Mat 10:29-31</reference> (note).
entries.5340c1c1dd1e76d7a106fbcf73666987b64ea58b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen40553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40554" type="x-p"/> Shall confess - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.32">Mat 10:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.33">Mat 10:33</reference> (note).
entries.89545843e8d788ddfbbac5f50ffc36dba84e5603: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen40554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40555" type="x-p"/> Him that blasphemeth - See the sin against the Holy Ghost explained, <reference osisRef="Mat.12.32">Mat 12:32</reference> (note).
entries.a9c7f471a8d07191f89fb86ad7e5d0b58d4bf088: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen40555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40556" type="x-p"/> Unto magistrates and powers - See <reference osisRef="Mat.10.17-Mat.10.20">Mat 10:17-20</reference>. <div eID="gen40556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40557" type="x-p"/> Take ye no thought - See <reference osisRef="Mat.6.25">Mat 6:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.10.19">Mat 10:19</reference>.
entries.5bce938291e18baf679894e8c9c4d6ded1ec3372: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen40557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40558" type="x-p"/> Speak to my brother, that he divide - Among the Jews, the children had the inheritance of their fathers divided among them; the eldest had a double portion, but all the rest had equal parts. It is likely the person complained of in the text was the elder brother; and he wished to keep the whole to himself - a case which is far from being uncommon. The spirit of covetousness cancels all bonds and obligations, makes wrong right, and cares nothing for father or brother.
entries.3e0e56868211c53c433e010ffec34cb5a35a1728: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen40558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40559" type="x-p"/> A judge - Without some judgment given in the case, no division could be made; therefore Jesus added the word judge. Pearce. A minister of Christ ought not to concern himself with secular affairs, any farther than charity and the order of discipline require it. Our Lord could have decided this difference in a moment; but the example of a perfect disengagement from worldly things was more necessary for the ministers of his Church than that of a charity applying itself to temporal concerns. He who preaches salvation to all should never make himself a party man; otherwise he loses the confidence, and consequently the opportunity of doing good to the party against whom he decides. Better to leave all these things to the civil magistrate, unless where a lawsuit may be prevented, and the matter decided to the satisfaction or acquiescence of both parties.
entries.4aaad00b57b4f78e9e816d8c2df2753cf6469fc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen40559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40560" type="x-p"/> Beware of covetousness - Or rather, Beware of all inordinate desires. I add πασης, all, on the authority of ABDKLM-Q, twenty-three others, both the Syriac, all the Persic, all the Arabic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate, all the Itala, and several of the primitive fathers. <div eID="gen40560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40561" type="x-p"/> Inordinate desires. Πλεονεξιας, from πλειον, more, and εχειν, to have; the desire to have more and more, let a person possess whatever he may. Such a disposition of mind is never satisfied; for, as soon as one object is gained, the heart goes out after another. <div eID="gen40561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40562" type="x-p"/> Consisteth not in the abundance - That is, dependeth not on the abundance. It is not superfluities that support man's life, but necessaries. What is necessary, God gives liberally; what is superfluous, he has not promised. Nor can a man's life be preserved by the abundance of his possessions: to prove this he spoke the following parable.
entries.d5ce2af151ca7a0e277d9a927ea72dccf1b25cd7: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen40562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40563" type="x-p"/> The ground of a certain rich man, etc. - He had generally what is called good luck in his farm, and this was a remarkably plentiful year.
entries.0d0ab762e3e8a043c374538ceba261f0fa4c82ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen40563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40564" type="x-p"/> He thought within himself - Began to be puzzled in consequence of the increase of his goods. Riches, though ever so well acquired, produce nothing but vexation and embarrassment.
entries.c589721cea0b9a2fd1a6ff3f6fb2d845a9569ba0: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen40564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40565" type="x-p"/> I will pull down, etc. - The rich are full of designs concerning this life, but in general take no thought about eternity till the time that their goods and their lives are both taken away.
entries.8eca0f785753e5c9baa542c17c39c9ab53c6598b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen40565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40566" type="x-p"/> Soul, thou hast much goods - Great possessions are generally accompanied with pride, idleness, and luxury; and these are the greatest enemies to salvation. Moderate poverty, as one justly observes, is a great talent in order to salvation; but it is one which nobody desires. <div eID="gen40566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40567" type="x-p"/> Take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry - This was exactly the creed of the ancient Atheists and Epicureans. Ede, bibe, lude; post mortem nulla voluptas. What a wretched portion for an immortal spirit! and yet those who know not God have no other, and many of them not even this.
entries.74bf832b854d544c11c0edd2bf3b64f64d08bedb: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen40567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40568" type="x-p"/> Thou fool! - To imagine that a man's comfort and peace can depend upon temporal things; or to suppose that these can satisfy the wishes of an immortal spirit! <div eID="gen40568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40569" type="x-p"/> This night - How awful was this saying! He had just made the necessary arrangements for the gratification of his sensual appetites; and, in the very night in which he had finally settled all his plans, his soul was called into the eternal world! What a dreadful awakening of a soul, long asleep in sin! He is now hurried into the presence of his Maker; none of his worldly goods can accompany him, and he has not a particle of heavenly treasure! There is a passage much like this in the book of Ecclesiasticus, 11:18, 19. There is that waxeth rich by his wariness and pinching, and this is the portion of his reward: Whereas he saith, I have found rest, and now will eat continually of my goods; and yet he knoweth not what time shall come upon him; and that he must leave those things to others, and die. We may easily see whence the above is borrowed.
entries.f261f8bf555034ed45ba337fbe994864a96775af: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen40569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40570" type="x-p"/> So is he - That is, thus will it be. This is not an individual case; all who make this life their portion, and who are destitute of the peace and salvation of God, shall, sooner or later, be surprised in the same way. <div eID="gen40570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40571" type="x-p"/> Layeth up treasure for himself - This is the essential characteristic of a covetous man: he desires riches; he gets them; he lays them up, not for the necessary uses to which they might be devoted, but for himself; to please himself, and to gratify his avaricious soul. Such a person is commonly called a miser, i.e. literally, a wretched, miserable man.
entries.57f96c1abe9c81a9a52a3c81f71a70badae7ef07: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen40571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40572" type="x-p"/> Take no thought - Be not anxiously careful. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.6.25">Mat 6:25</reference> (note).
entries.e9d876ba05ee57d188616c2d6a9170bb0889a31b: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen40572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40573" type="x-p"/> To his stature one cubit? - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.6.27">Mat 6:27</reference> (note).
entries.41c8d39dffbfca22fc12146df71976d91294b1c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen40573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40574" type="x-p"/> Into the oven - See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.6.30">Mat 6:30</reference>.
entries.b3a89e90749a4d58e1131592052c05de36a40ae7: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen40574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40575" type="x-p"/> Neither be ye of doubtful mind - Or, in anxious suspense, μη μετεωριζεσθε. Raphelius gives several examples to prove that the meaning of the word is, to have the mind agitated with useless thoughts, and vain imaginations concerning food, raiment, and riches, accompanied with perpetual uncertainty.
entries.95ef029908856388a7d4d3217388bb547faed1dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen40575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40576" type="x-p"/> The nations of the world seek after - Or, earnestly seek, επιζητει from επι above, over, and ζητεω, I seek; to seek one thing after another, to be continually and eagerly coveting. This is the employment of the nations of this world, utterly regardless of God and eternity! It is the essence of heathenism to live only for this life; and it is the property of Christianity to lead men to live here in reference to another and better world. Reader! how art thou living? <div eID="gen40576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40577" type="x-p"/> Dr. Lightfoot observes on this place, that κοσμος, the world, and αιων, world or age, have a meaning in the sacred writings which they have not in profane authors. Αιων has relation to the Jewish ages, and κοσμος to the ages that are not Jewish: hence, by συντελεια του αιωνος, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.3">Mat 24:3</reference>, is meant the end of the Jewish age or world: and προ χρονων αιωνιων, <reference osisRef="Tit.1.2">Tit 1:2</reference>, means before the Jewish world began; and hence it is that the term world is very often, in the New Testament, to be understood only of the Gentiles.
entries.0605785e7206f8df4ce89e4e5be9400f326ec2aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen40577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40578" type="x-p"/> Fear not, little flock - Or, very little flock, το μικρον ποιμνιον. This is what some term a double diminutive, and, literally translated, is, little little flock. Though this refers solely to the apostles and first believers, of whom it was literally true, yet we may say that the number of genuine believers has been, and is still, small, in comparison of heathens and false Christians. <div eID="gen40578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40579" type="x-p"/> It is your Father's good pleasure - Ευδοκησεν, It hath pleased, etc., though this tense joined with an infinitive has often the force of the present. Our Lord intimated, God has already given you that kingdom which consists in righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost, and has undertaken to protect and save you to the uttermost; therefore, fear not; the smallness of your number cannot hurt you, for omnipotence itself has undertaken your cause.
entries.9b80b24a0dda9a45483e03dae8e9449d93f546e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen40579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40580" type="x-p"/> Sell that ye have - Dispose of your goods. Be not like the foolish man already mentioned, who laid up the produce of his fields, without permitting the poor to partake of God's bounty: turn the fruits of your fields (which are beyond what you need for your own support) into money, and give it in alms; and the treasure thus laid out, shall be as laid up for yourselves and families in heaven. This purse shall not grow old, and this treasure shill not decay. Ye shall by and by find both the place where you laid up the treasure, and the treasure itself in the place; for he who hath pity on the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and he may rest assured, that whatever, for Christ's sake, he thus lays out, it will be paid him again.
entries.467a5243578e7700bf3d62d32ad31999cc284f11: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen40580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40581" type="x-p"/> Where your treasure is - Men fix their hearts on their treasures, and often resort to the place where they have deposited them, to see that all is safe and secure. Let God be the treasure of your soul, and let your heart go frequently to the place where his honor dwelleth. There is a curious parallel passage to this in Plautus, quoted by Bishop Pearce on <reference osisRef="Mat.6.21">Mat 6:21</reference>. Nam ego sum hic; animus domi est, sc. cum argento meo. "I am here; but my heart is at home, i.e. with my money."
entries.6130f483c74bfe5c0f66f314e9d40fa11fb4a909: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen40581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40582" type="x-p"/> Let your loins - Be active, diligent, determined ready; let all hinderances be removed out of the way; and let the candle of the Lord be always found burning brightly in your hand. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.12.37">Luk 12:37</reference> (note).
entries.859fa95b62adb46f776d7997624a79725dfebe8f: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen40582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40583" type="x-p"/> That wait for their lord - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.25.1">Mat 25:1</reference> (note), etc. <div eID="gen40583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40584" type="x-p"/> The wedding - How the Jewish weddings were celebrated, see in the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.8.12">Mat 8:12</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mat.22.11">Mat 22:11</reference> (note).
entries.1d5c6940e40809933a0efc2ecc93ed3a9880c5d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen40584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40585" type="x-p"/> He shall gird himself - Alluding to the long garments which were worn in the eastern countries; and which, in travelling and serving, were tucked up in their belts. That those among the Romans who waited on the company at table were girded, and had their clothes tucked up, appears from what Horace says, Sat. b. vi. l. 107: Veluti Succinctus cursitat Hospes, He runs about like a girded waiter. The host himself often performed this office. And ibid. viii. 10: Puer alle cinctus: and that the same custom prevailed among the Jews appears from <reference osisRef="Joh.13.4">Joh 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.5">Joh 13:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Luk.17.8">Luk 17:8</reference>. From this verse we may gather likewise, that it was the custom of those days, as it was, not long since, among us, for the bridegroom, at the wedding supper, to wait as a servant upon the company. See Bishop Pearce.
entries.405deb06dbed5adfdb83fe49ef2a13ce42ee793f: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen40585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40586" type="x-p"/> If he shall come in the second watch - See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.25">Mat 14:25</reference>.
entries.23ed2425ceb3b86e21a82ff4ff68a745f8cfa14e: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen40586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40587" type="x-p"/> Be ye therefore ready also - It is pretty evident that what is related here, from <reference osisRef="Luk.12.35">Luk 12:35</reference> to <reference osisRef="Luk.12.49">Luk 12:49</reference>, was spoken by our Lord at another time. See <reference osisRef="Mat.24.42">Mat 24:42</reference> (note), etc., and the notes there.
entries.1d8d6381e3e77bb7cdbd61e42658af6eb00eeed8: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen40587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40588" type="x-p"/> Faithful and wise steward - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.24.45">Mat 24:45</reference> (note); where the several parts of the steward's office are mentioned and explained. Those appear to have been stewards among the Jews, whose business it was to provide all the members of a family, not only with food, but with raiment.
entries.a759d2f70c6f45e9cd7a19657fabdc5d6b83774b: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen40588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40589" type="x-p"/> Begin to beat, etc. - See the different parts of this bad minister's conduct pointed out on <reference osisRef="Mat.24.48">Mat 24:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.49">Mat 24:49</reference> (note).
entries.c1a61d715c3a8301329919828b67470a38cdbd83: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen40589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40590" type="x-p"/> With the unbelievers - Or, rather, the unfaithful; των σπιϚων. Persons who had the light and knowledge of God's word, but made an improper use of the privileges they received. The persons mentioned here differ widely from unbelievers or infidels, viz. those who were in a state of heathenism, because they had not the revelation of the Most High: the latter knew not the will of God, <reference osisRef="Luk.12.48">Luk 12:48</reference>, and, though they acted against it, did not do it in obstinacy; the former knew that will, and daringly opposed it. They were unfaithful, and therefore heavily punished.
entries.e9c58ab857c934a1704f94aa118179ff09da167a: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen40590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40591" type="x-p"/> Shall be beaten with many stripes - Criminals among the Jews could not be beaten with more than forty stripes; and as this was the sum of the severity to which a whipping could extend, it may be all that our Lord here means. But, in some cases, a man was adjudged to receive fourscore stripes! How could this be, when the law had decreed only forty? Answer: By doubling the crime. He received forty for each crime; if he were guilty of two offenses, he might receive fourscore. See Lightfoot.
entries.25e63ae1fef6450c764e592d4edd14bbbc1b49ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen40591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40592" type="x-p"/> Shall be beaten with few - For petty offenses the Jews in many cases inflicted so few as four, five, and six stripes. See examples in Lightfoot. <div eID="gen40592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40593" type="x-p"/> From this and the preceding verse we find that it is a crime to be ignorant of God's will; because to every one God has given less or more of the means of instruction. Those who have had much light, or the opportunity of receiving much, and have not improved it to their own salvation, and the good of others, shall have punishment proportioned to the light they have abused. On the other hand, those who have had little light, and few means of improvement, shall have few stripes, shall be punished only for the abuse of the knowledge they possessed. See at the end of the chapter.
entries.c0b5e513f620b9c76bb8b350b15f3a50a0ee62b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen40593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40594" type="x-p"/> I am come to send fire - See this subject largely explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.34">Mat 10:34</reference> (note), etc. From the connection in which these words stand, both in this place and in Matthew, it appears as if our Lord intended by the word fire, not only the consuming influence of the Roman sword, but also the influence of his own Spirit in the destruction of sin. In both these senses this fire was already kindled: as yet, however, it appeared but as a spark, but was soon to break out into an all-consuming flame.
entries.0c54db137506dd703a318c11df6a90d629a8898e: <hi type="bold">Verse 50</hi> <div eID="gen40594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40595" type="x-p"/> But I have a baptism - The fire, though already kindled, cannot burn up till after the Jews have put me to death: then the Roman sword shall come, and the Spirit of judgment, burning, and purification shall be poured out.
entries.bddbdda6418b2c77a53d45cfb495836daaeb2251: <hi type="bold">Verse 51</hi> <div eID="gen40595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40596" type="x-p"/> To give peace - See <reference osisRef="Mat.10.34">Mat 10:34</reference>.
entries.da1a36a0898759c518827be7b5a5ceff64bb5f48: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen40596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40597" type="x-p"/> Five in one house divided - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.35">Mat 10:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.36">Mat 10:36</reference> (note).
entries.73d49cbf920876c4a428ea310e91cdbcedf9a32e: <hi type="bold">Verse 54</hi> <div eID="gen40597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40598" type="x-p"/> A cloud rise - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.16.2">Mat 16:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.3">Mat 16:3</reference> (note).
entries.1de5c63f5247793e777eafdd69e96486d20f27f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 56</hi> <div eID="gen40598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40599" type="x-p"/> This time? - Can ye not discover from the writings of the prophets, and from the events which now take place, that this is the time of the Messiah, and that I am the very person foretold by them?
entries.fc60d80462f50f2c77802357bab5142a9363dfb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 57</hi> <div eID="gen40599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40600" type="x-p"/> And why - judge ye - Even without the express declarations of the prophets, ye might, from what ye see and hear yourselves, discern that God has now visited his people in such a manner as he never did before.
entries.e99fe59e10d3e0a285b5b6e9db2bcc20c1317353: <hi type="bold">Verse 58</hi> <div eID="gen40600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40601" type="x-p"/> When thou goest with thine adversary - This and the next verse are a part of our Lord's sermon upon the mount. See them explained <reference osisRef="Mat.5.25">Mat 5:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.5.26">Mat 5:26</reference> (note). St. Luke is very particular in collecting and relating every word and action of our blessed Lord, but seldom gives them in the order of time in which they were spoken or done. See the Preface to this Gospel. <div eID="gen40601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40602" type="x-p"/> Give diligence - Δος εργασιαν, Give labor, do every thing in thy power to get free before a suit commences. <div eID="gen40602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40603" type="x-p"/> The officer - Πρακτωρ properly signifies such an officer as was appointed to levy the fines imposed by the law for a violation of any of its precepts. See Kypke.
entries.bc822aa13e7364ef0ecbae36a5f6004fbce4c431: <hi type="bold">Verse 59</hi> <div eID="gen40603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40604" type="x-p"/> Till thou hast paid the very last mite - And when can this be, if we understand the text spiritually? Can weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth, pay to Divine justice the debt a sinner has contracted? This is impossible: let him who readeth understand. <div eID="gen40604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40605" type="x-p"/> The subject of the 47th and 48th verses has been greatly misunderstood, and has been used in a very dangerous manner. Many have thought that their ignorance of Divine things would be a sufficient excuse for their crimes; and, that they might have but few stripes, they voluntarily continued in ignorance. But such persons should know that God will judge them for the knowledge they might have received, but refused to acquire. No criminal is excused because he has been ignorant of the laws of his country, and so transgressed them, when it can be proved that those very laws have been published throughout the land. Much knowledge is a dangerous thing if it be not improved; as this will greatly aggravate the condemnation of its possessor. Nor will it avail a person, in the land of light and information, to be ignorant, as he shall be judged for what he might have known; and, perhaps, in this case, the punishment of this voluntarily ignorant man will be even greater than that of the more enlightened; because his crimes are aggravated by this consideration, that he refused to have the light, that he might neither be obliged to walk in the light, nor account for the possession of it. So we find that the plea of ignorance is a mere refuge of lies, and none can plead it who has the book of God within his reach, and lives in a country blessed with the preaching of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.  <chapter eID="Luke.12"/> <div eID="gen40605" type="x-p"/>

entries.a1277caa92134015bc10d09a90b2affbfabae4fa:
Verse 1. In the mean time. While he was discoursing with the scribes and Pharisees, as recorded in the last chapter.

An innumerable multitude. The original word is myriads, or ten thousands. It is used here to signify that there was a great crowd or collection of people, who were anxious to hear him. Multitudes were attracted to the Saviour's ministry, and it is worthy of remark that he never had more to hear him than when he was most faithful and severe in his reproofs of sinners. Men's consciences are on the side of the faithful reprover of their sins; and though they deeply feel the reproof, yet they will still respect and hear him that reproves.

To his disciples, first of all. This does not mean that his disciples were, before all others, to avoid hypocrisy, but that this was the first or chief thing of which they were to beware. The meaning is this:

"He said to his disciples, Above all things beware," &c.

The leaven. Mt 16:6.

Which is hypocrisy. Mt 7:5. Hypocrisy is like leaven or yeast, because--

1st. It may exist without being immediately detected. Leaven mixed in flour is not known until it produces its effects.

2nd. It is insinuating. Leaven will soon pervade the whole mass. So hypocrisy will, if undetected and unremoved, soon pervade all our exercises and feelings.

3rd. It is swelling. It puffs us up, and fills us with pride and vanity. No man is more proud than the hypocrite, and none is more odious to God. When Jesus cautions them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, he means that they should be cautious about imbibing their spirit and becoming like them. The religion of Jesus is one of sincerity, of humility, of an entire want of disguise. The humblest man is the best Christian, and he who has the least disguise is most like his Master.

Verse 3. Shall be proclaimed upon the housetops. Mt 20:27. The custom of making proclamation from the tops or roofs of houses still prevails in the East. Dr. Thomson (The Land and the Book, vol. i. p. 51, 52) says:

"At the present day, local governors in country
districts cause their commands thus to be published.
Their proclamations are generally made in the evening,
after the people have returned from their labours in
the field. The public crier ascends the highest
roof at hand, and lifts up his voice in a long-drawn
call upon all faithful subjects to give ear and obey.
He then proceeds to announce, in a set form,
the will of their master, and demand obedience thereto."

Verse 13. One of the company. One of the multitude. This man had probably had a dispute with his brother, supposing that his brother had refused to do him justice. Conceiving that Jesus had power over the people--that what he said must be performed--he endeavoured to secure him on his side of the dispute and gain his point. From the parable which follows, it would appear that he had no just claim on the inheritance, but was influenced by covetousness. Besides, if he had any just claim, it might have been secured by the laws of the land.

Speak to my brother. Command my brother.

Divide the inheritance. An inheritance is the property which is left by a father to his children. Among the Jews the older brother had two shares, or twice as much as any other child, De 21:17. The remainder was then equally divided among all the children.

(m) "Master, speak to my brother" Eze 33:31
entries.8414b1587b0ba6c1281198fb0ca3be1d75eb9daf:
Verse 14. Who made me a judge? It is not my business to settle controversies of this kind. They are to be settled by the magistrate. Jesus came for another purpose--to preach the gospel, and so to bring men to a willingness to do right. Civil affairs are to be left to the magistrate. There is no doubt that Jesus could have told him what was right in this case, but then it would have been interfering with the proper office of the magistrates; it might have led him into controversy with the Jews; and it was, besides, evidently apart from the proper business of his life. We may remark, also, that the appropriate business of ministers of the gospel is to attend to spiritual concerns. They should have little to do with the temporal matters of the people. If they can persuade men who are at variance to be reconciled, it is right; but they have no power to take the place of a magistrate, and to settle contentions in a legal way.

(n) "Man, who made me a judge" Jn 18:25

Verse 15. Beware of covetousness. One of these brothers, no doubt, was guilty of this sin; and our Saviour, as was his custom, took occasion to warn his disciples of its danger.

Covetousness. An unlawful desire of the property of another; also a desire of gain or riches beyond what is necessary for our wants. It is a violation of the tenth commandment (Ex 20:17), and is expressly called idolatry (Col 3:5). Compare, also, Eph 5:3, Heb 13:5.

A man's life. The word life is sometimes taken in the sense of happiness or felicity, and some have supposed this to be the meaning here, and that Jesus meant to say that a man's comfort does not depend on affluence--that is, on more than is necessary for his daily wants; but this meaning does not suit the parable following, which is designed to show that property will not lengthen out a man's life, and therefore is not too ardently to be sought, and is of little value. The word life, therefore, is to be taken literally.

Consisteth not. Rather, dependeth not on his possessions. His possessions will not prolong it. The passage, then, means: Be not anxious about obtaining wealth, for, however much you may obtain, it will not prolong your life. That depends on the will of God, and it requires something besides wealth to make us ready to meet him. This sentiment he proceeds to illustrate by a beautiful parable.

entries.cd17af60f7f9be945e970e51adf51bcae3ddf8ac:
Verse 17. He thought within himself. He reasoned or inquired. He was anxious and perplexed. Riches increase thought and perplexity. Indeed, this is almost their only effect--to engross the thoughts and steal the heart away from better things, in order to take care of the useless wealth.

Verse 18. I will pull down my barns. The word barns, here, properly means, granaries, or places exclusively designed to put wheat, barley, &c. They were commonly made, by the ancients, underground, where grain could be kept a long time more safe from thieves and from vermin. If it be asked why he did not let the old ones remain and build new ones, it may be answered that it would be easier to enlarge those already excavated in the earth than to dig new ones.
